subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
At the outset, Mr. Speaker, I should like to add my congratulations to those numerous congratulations which have already been extended to our new Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) during the course of this debate, both upon the content of his budget and upon his very excellent presentation of it. It is natural, I think, that anyone from Nova Scotia should have a particular interest in the finance portfolio. First, of course, we have a strong Scottish leaven in our population, and as you know the Scot is a notoriously canny financier. Secondly, if you consider the list of distinguished men who have held that portfolio from time to time since confederation you will find that on that list there is a surprising sprinkling of the names of Nova Scotians, beginning with Tupper and coming down to as recent a time as Mr. Ilsley's. Consequently, we from Nova Scotia have a very particular interest in any incumbent of that position. I think I can pay the present minister no higher compliment than to say that on the basis of his budget he has left no room whatever for doubt that he is a worthy successor, not only to his immediate predecessor the Hon. Douglas Abbott, but also to all those capable and distinguished statesmen who have in the past carried out the onerous duties which now devolve upon him. I offer him my most hearty congratulations.
Compared with the budgets of the last few years this one in contemplating a deficit has an element, I think, of boldness, of experiment and of flexibility. Certainly it should silence that cry which we occasionally hear from the opposition benches that this administration is too set in its ways ever to depart from the beaten path. I think this is a departure. Then, too, in the light of the public reception which this budget has been given
The Budget-Mr. Lusby I think it has been amply demonstrated that this government is still intent upon carrying out the wishes of the people, a fundamental principle of our democracy. In spite of whatever the opposition may choose to say, my observations over the course of the last few weeks have convinced me this is definitely a popular budget. It has received considered approval from the vast majority of Canadians and, whatever opposition members may choose to think, the people are usually right- or else how could our democracy survive?
Indeed, when I contrast the public reception which has been accorded to this budget with the railing from the opposition benches against it-here I am not in the least impugning their right to rail, and perhaps it is even their duty-I am inclined to wonder how the opposition members could dare to trust in the validity of their own arguments. Naturally, when the budget debate is on, the order of the day in the opposition ranks is, "curse the budget", if I may say that. But I wonder if many of the opposition stalwarts, as they go to work loyally in this debate, have not entertained feelings somewhat akin to that ancient biblical character Balaam, incidentally a false prophet, when he was invited to curse Jacob and defy Israel. He did not fancy the assignment. In any event, to curse what the people have not cursed, to denounce what they have approved, is never an easy task in a democratic country such as this, and those who are attempting it are meeting, I think, with a deserved lack of success both within this chamber and without.
In my opinion, this budget has gained the approval of the intelligent and informed citizen in this country, not primarily because it represents a substantial saving to him in income and other taxes but because he is firmly convinced that these changes which it has brought about will achieve their primary purpose of stimulating the national economy. I agree with that belief; I expect these changes to exert a substantial influence in this regard by virtue of the additional purchasing power which they make available. As the minister indicated in presenting the budget, national fiscal policy is an important means of promoting economic stability and expansion. I am convinced that in his capable hands it will prove to be an instrument skilfully and successfully applied for that purpose.
There are one or two points upon which I am not entirely in accord with the provisions of the budget. For example, I should have preferred to see the special excise tax on soft drinks and the like eliminated or at least further reduced, so as to avoid any suggestion of unfairness. Not strictly in the budgetary

The Budget-Mr. Lusby field but arising out of the measures taken there, is the question whether, in view of the reduction of 5 per cent in the excise tax upon automobiles, the dealers across the country should not be given some relief in respect of any losses they have sustained in connection with vehicles purchased by them before the budget was brought down. I realize that the decision of the Department of National Revenue, as announced by the Minister of Finance, is in line with the usual policy in such situations. But I have since had representations from a number of dealers in my constituency, and I suppose the situation is very much the same all over the country, and I find that substantial amounts are involved in each case. And as between the practical impossibility of making a rebate in every case of a reduction in excise or sales tax and the exigencies of the situation in which the automobile dealers now find themselves, it is my thought that possibly, without setting any binding precedent, some suitable ground of compromise might be found in this instance.
In presenting the budget the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) made an announcement to which, as a representative from a maritime constituency, I pay particular attention. That was the announcement that a royal commission is to be appointed to examine carefully into and report upon the future economic prospects of this country. The minister has mentioned among the contemplated aspects of the commission's work such matters as the charting of probable developments both in our productive capacities and our external markets, an examination of population growth, and the magnitude and nature of our future requirements. Although, as he said, it is not intended that the commission shall make a long series of detailed policy recommendations, I assume that one of its fundamental purposes will be the assembling of material upon which the government may base its economic policies of the future.
It seems to me that this sort of national inventory and stock-taking at this time with regard to our economic future is an excellent project indeed. And in this connection I should like to point out that one of the greatest of the internal problems which this country faces, and must continue to face, is that of effectively maintaining a reasonably equitable balance of economic development and activity in all its parts. I said a moment ago that as a representative of a maritime constituency I took a particular interest in the minister's announcement that this commission was to be set up. Why? Because I see the possibility that through its work may come some positive indication as to how this government, in conjunction with

our maritime provincial and municipal governments, and all other bodies which may be concerned, may best work in order to ensure for the maritime provinces their fair share in that mighty economic and industrial development and expansion already far under way in so many parts of this country- a development and expansion which, barring perhaps the disasters of war, will continue as surely as the sun is going to rise tomorrow.
In its over-all national aspects, our future is such as to rejoice the heart of every Canadian. But I need hardly say, Mr. Speaker, that it is of relatively little importance to an unemployed coal miner in Nova Scotia, for instance, to know that the oil industry in Alberta is flourishing, and its prospects are bright. And I have referred to the oil industry only as an example. It is imperative that some means be found, some policy adopted, which will ensure to the maritime provinces a fair share in the prospective national economic and industrial development, a reasonable level of prosperity as compared with those provinces which, by virtue of greater population, central geographic position-which is one of the most important items-endowment of natural resources, or other advantages which we in the maritimes lack, are now far in the lead.
Perhaps I should say here, Mr. Speaker, that I do not wish to be accused of pessimism. I am not at all unmindful of the many bright spots in the maritime picture. Just last night the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robi-chaud) gave us a description of the astounding development of base metal mining in northern New Brunswick, which is now in assured and immediate prospect. That is perhaps the most encouraging event that province has ever seen. The intensive search for similar metals in Nova Scotia, which has been carried on for some time and is still being carried on, gives ground for hope that at least to some extent we may enjoy a similar boon.
It is my firm belief, too, that in the years ahead our forest industries, our fisheries and our tourist trade will grow to be of increasing importance, and will reflect a far higher level of activity than has generally been the case in the past. Nor am I one to fear that any development in some other part of Canada-and at the moment I am thinking particularly of the St. Lawrence seaway development-taking the long-term view, will injure us in the maritime provinces. My view is entirely to the contrary.
But in certain aspects, notably-and I think this is the chief one-in the field of the development of manufacturing and other secondary industries, I think it is perfectly

true to say that our economy has not overcome its traditional lag as compared with other parts of Canada.
Therefore I suggest to the Minister of Finance, to the government and to the House of Commons, that one of the first and fundamental objectives of any such royal commission as is proposed should be the assembling of all available facts and figures which may make possible the formulation of policies designed to redress, so far as conceivably it can be done, that regional imbalance of economic development, industrial activity and resulting opportunity and prosperity which now exists as between various regions of this country and which to my mind, as I have said, is one of the real internal problems which beset us as a nation.
In an earlier speech in the house during this session I made the suggestion that some permanent federal agency might well be set up or designated to keep under constant watch the peculiar difficulties with which we in the maritimes contend in our economic and industrial life and, acting in conjunction with all provincial or other bodies having the same interests, to devise and recommend such measures as from time to time may seem advisable further to overcome those difficulties.
The royal commission outlined by the Minister of Finance is not, I take it, intended to be a permanent body, or even a quasipermanent body, although I assume its activities will be carried on over a considerable period of time. However, I do urge most strongly that it be directed during its lifetime to devote a full share of detailed attention to the economic prospects of the maritimes, the bright as well as the dark. Indeed, I think it might well set up a distinct subcommittee to deal with that aspect of its work.
One or two aspects of our maritime economic and industrial life, however, require in my opinion an entirely separate study. First of all is the state of the coal mining industry, which urgently-and I repeat the word "urgently"-requires immediate consideration. Such consideration would consist largely of correlating known facts and, upon the basis of those facts, making recommendations for action. The urgency of the situation is starkly emphasized by the threatened closing of No. 1-B colliery at Glace Bay, Cape Breton, which is one of the most important coal mines in the province.
We know of course that the first problem of the coal industry in Nova Scotia is the increasing competition from other fuels. We
The Budget-Mr. Lusby also know, however, that coal is still the chief source of fuel energy in Canada, and that in the event of war assured Canadian sources of supply would become vital at once to the safety of this country.
In certain fields, such as that of the coal fired gas turbine engine, there is the prospect-unfortunately at the present time it is not much more than that-that coal may again become fully competitive with oil. There is the possibility that new and more efficient processes may be discovered for the extraction on a commercially profitable basis of the endless variety of chemicals and other by-products which are known to be available from coal.
Then we have the often repeated forecast of the dominion coal board that by the middle 1960's, if our coal industry survives the difficult intermediate period, Canadian industrial expansion, in spite of the inroads of other fuels, will provide an assured market for coal sufficient to maintain activity in our mines at least at something like its present level. I hardly need add that a coal mine once closed is very unlikely to be reopened. After considering all these things, Mr. Speaker, I submit that the preservation of the Canadian coal mining industry-and I of course am thinking more of the Nova Scotia segment of it, upon which the livelihood of perhaps a fifth of our total provincial population depends-is a matter of national concern and merits the utmost efforts of all, management, labour, the provincial government and the federal government. Each one of these has its part to play if the industry is to be preserved.
If the forecast of the dominion coal board is correct-and I think for the present we must assume that premise-the problem is to tide the industry over the difficult years immediately ahead. I suggest a concerted effort by all those concerned to devise a workable plan for the preservation of the industry at approximately its present level over that period. Call it a ten-year plan, if you like. That may be slightly reminiscent of our friends in Russia, but certainly if such a plan can prevent poverty and unemployment in the coal industry you cannot find a better defence against the inroads of communism.
Another matter which is of some concern, at least of some interest, to the maritimes- and which I strongly think deserves a separate study by a separate royal commission-is the construction of the Chignecto canal. Such a study would determine once and for all the benefits which might reasonably be expected to accrue to this country and particularly to the maritimes if the canal became a reality. No such commission has been appointed by the federal government since the

The Budget-Mr. Lusby 1930's. In view of the great changes that have taken place, I believe a thorough study of present-day conditions should be made by such a commission. Once and for all it would settle the question whether the benefits which would accrue would justify the cost of construction and maintenance. I have urged before in this house the desirability of such a study by such a commission as the only proper means of settling this longstanding question. Only the other day my friend and colleague, the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Murphy), whose constituency, when the canal is completed, will be on the bank opposite to mine, raised the matter at some length in this very debate. I have no wish to repeat the statistics which he has placed upon the records of the house from time to time, but I do wish to say that there are weighty arguments in favour of the canal which deserve the careful and sympathetic consideration of a competent and authorized body.
Before I conclude, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say I am happy to note that the budget makes several tariff reductions which will be of benefit to this country's farmers. Agriculture remains, in my opinion, the real foundation of this country's economy. 1 should like at this time also to commend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) upon the further extension of the price support program for butter, a measure which is of very real assistance to the dairy farmer.
In my constituency the role played by the federal Department of Agriculture in the promotion of efficient farming methods is particularly well known because we have a dominion experimental farm at Nappan, on the very edge of the marshlands which are the subject of the maritime marshlands reclamation project. During the Easter recess I had an opportunity to visit the farm and to find out something about the work that is being carried on there in order to promote the raising of beef cattle, not only on those marshes but elsewhere in Nova Scotia. In fact, on that very day there was a well-attended group meeting there of farmers interested in these subjects. It was just a coincidence that I was there.
Since it is highly desirable that the most profitable use available shall be made of the reclaimed marshlands, I hope the department will continue to carry on and expand its research into the possibilities of beef raising on those lands as well as on other lands in Nova Scotia.
In conclusion, I should just like to say that the work of such a royal commission as the Minister of Finance has in contemplation would certainly be far from complete if it
IMr. Lusby.]
did not include as one of the most important items on its agenda a thorough study and assessment of the future prospects and possibilities of agriculture in every part of this country where arable land is available.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to traverse much of the ground which has been covered already. However, there are a number of matters to which I intend to refer which up to the present moment have not been dealt with or, if dealt with, have been dealt with only generally.
I want to say immediately to the minister that I congratulate him on having brought in his first budget; as Harris came in, Lord Keynes went out. There has been a complete transition in the philosophy that heretofore activated the government, a change of point of view, an alteration of direction and in effect an admission of the validity of the criticisms which we of the official opposition have been advancing in recent years.
At the beginning I am just going to say a word in regard to employment. Strangely enough, there has been no serious answer from the government regarding the unemployment problem that still fills the hearts of many Canadians, no answer whatever as to what is to be done now by the government, except a speech by the Prime Minister at the dominion-provincial conference as to what is to be expected at a further meeting to take place this coming fall between the federal and provincial authorities. For some reason or other the plans of 1945, the green book of that day and all that it stood for and the principles which in a measure contributed to the success of the government at the polls in two subsequent elections, now have been set aside, departed from, forgotten. Indeed, the great and abiding principles that were to bring about a new millennium in dominion and provincial relations now have been embalmed in the records of history.
I intend to make a general reference to the budget, and to mention a few suggestions as to matters that might be dealt with and should be dealt with at this time. First, I wish to make reference to a purely western condition. After years of drought periodically occurring in the western provinces, today we in Saskatchewan, and to a lesser degree in Manitoba, have suffered a disaster, the like of which I have not seen in the many years that I have been in western Canada. During the days of the 1930's larger areas were devastated by drought; now there is need of immediate action by the federal government because of floods. I see no reason why there should be such unnecessary delay in determining whether or not what has taken place

is a national emergency. I believe that what has taken place in Saskatchewan, and to a lesser degree in Manitoba, is far and beyond any responsibility that should rest upon the provinces. The costs of rehabilitation should be assumed in considerable measure by the federal government.
There were great hopes on budget night. The minister made his speech and reports went across the country that income taxpayers would save 13 or 14 per cent across the board. However, when examined in the light of the actual circumstances and reviewed carefully, as it was by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) in his opening speech, the hopes of budget night have been dissipated in subsequent days.
The sales tax stays upon the needs of the home and upon almost everything but food. The hon. member who has just resumed his seat referred to the help being given to agriculture in the tariff reductions. There are a few reductions which will benefit limited areas of agricultural endeavour, but generally speaking the budget holds out no material benefit for Canadian agriculture or for reductions in the cost of production of Canadian agriculture.
As far as the income tax is concerned, the meagreness of the reductions will be realized only when the deductions commence to be made-small, trivial, unimportant. The reduction in the excise tax on automobiles is a worthy step, but it is only a step. With automobiles being the necessity they are, a 5 per cent reduction in no way meets the situation and the government ought to have gone considerably further than they did.
As I mentioned a moment ago, the sales tax remains, and the taxes on television and radio remain. The costs of government are on the increase in every department of government as far as I can read the record, with the exception of agriculture, defence production and national defence. There are increases in expenditures when there should be reductions. Agricultural expenditures are reduced by some $25 million; defence production by $28 million; and national defence by $118 million. The total reduction in expenditures this year for all departments is $95 million, which indicates that in the other departments of government there have been substantial increases.
I think one of the purposes of this budget was to spread plenty of little among many, not to attack the need for immediate action to be taken which would bring about the restoration of lost markets and provide an impetus to trade within our country by reducing costs through lower taxes, but simply to thinly spread a series of small
The Budget-Mr. Diefenbaker benefits to the few. The budget will not have the effect of bringing about a restoration of impetus and an encouragement to initiative.
Some have spoken of Canada receiving a shot in the arm by the budget, but on examination it is shown that what Canadians have received from this budget is merely a scratch on the arm. There has been plenty of little spread among the many but without sufficient emphasis in any particular to encourage the expansion and development of industry.
Costs of government have not been cut.
I should like to quote what Mr. J. A. Calder, president of the Canadian Manufacturers Association, said in a statement he made in St. John's, Newfoundland. The article states:
He said that in five years, from 1943 to 1953, government spending rose to 18-1 per cent of the gross national product from 11-5 per cent.
He went on to point out that corporate taxes had not been reduced to any extent.
I remember so well past years when Mr. Abbott referred to the dangerous situation when corporate taxation was exacting almost 50 per cent of the amount being made by corporate business. Such high taxation establishes a socialist system under the free enterprise system. Mr. Calder went on to say that there were not sufficient economies in government; there was no lowering of corporate taxes which would attract more venture capital which would mean increased productivity and lower prices, which would mean increased sales, which increased sales would more than offset any loss of government income.
The government has chosen to do very little at a time when drastic action is necessary. There are three or four things which I think the government could have done at this time and should have done. I have mentioned one, the removal of the sales tax upon the needs of the home. The cost of living continues to rise. According to the records of the bureau of statistics of May 4, there had been an increase in the previous month to 116-1 from 116. It reports rising prices for flour, tea, eggs, potatoes, fresh fruits, gasoline, etc. There can be no justification for the maintenance of the unusually high sales tax upon the needs of the home.
What business needs to meet the challenge of international markets, of improved techniques of production, is tax relief for programs of research. West Germany is once more in the family of nations, a step forward which may establish the certainty of peace in Europe, an act of faith which is already having its effect. It must be realized that West Germany is the third trading nation in the world, and as she will now be free to establish her steamship lines, her air lines and

The Budget-Mr. Diefenbaker the like, the competition of recent months and years is bound to be intensified.
Last year business in the United States spent more than $3,000 million upon research designed to enhance competition in export markets, to preserve the domestic market against the competition of low-economy countries, and to meet the problem of dwindling resources. Canada can do no less. The government of this country should give encouragement to research development on the part of industry by extending the degree by which such expenditures may be deducted when determining liability for income tax. If Canadian industry is to compete it cannot afford to be a mere rubber stamp producer of commodities developed by research in the United States. Encouragement should be given to an extension of the field of research so that expenditures in that direction may be deducted as a proper expense.
Third, one means of encouraging the expansion of jobs is to encourage industry to expand its physical equipment in the form of buildings, machinery and the like. That can be achieved and was achieved during the days of war by accelerated depreciation allowances. The same course is needed now to provide the encouragement that expansion will assure and also to increase employment within this country.
Statisticians say that it requires a million dollars of capital investment to provide 117 extra jobs. If all the savings that are to be effected this year by the 2 per cent reduction in corporation tax were translated into jobs, it would mean an increase of only 3,000 jobs in toto. If the government would give encouragement to industry to expand in this way, many jobs would be created.
Fourth, I regret that the minister has not seen fit to reform the obsolete, unjust and unjustifiable provisions of the succession duty act. There is an act that represents in some particulars a disregard of the rights of the individual. There are anomalies. Anyone who has had experience with the operation of the act knows of them. There is the injustice that affects many people in this country, whereby if one's share is $1 less than $50,000 there is no liability, but if it is $1 over $50,000 the full amount becomes liable to the impact of the tax. There are also provisions regarding pensions and annuities being capitalized which were never intended to be interpreted in the manner in which they are today. They have the effect of operating as a bar to the development of our country and also a discouragement to those who, through thrift, endeavour to better themselves and protect their dependents.
fMr. Diefenbaker.]

There are many members of this house with ability that is not being used, reservoirs of capacity that are available, who understand the operation of the succession duty act. A committee could be set up of such members who would hear the representations made by the officials of his department and of the Department of National Revenue and it could recommend changes in the act that would maintain to a greater degree the equities that should prevail and would also assure to a greater extent justice in the administration of the act.
Next, I am one of those who believe that, to discourage the drift toward socialism, something should be done to encourage individuals in this country to save so as to build up their own pension systems, by permitting them within limits to deduct the annual payments they make for the purpose of providing themselves with retirement pensions. I went into considerable detail in this matter with one of the outstanding chartered accountants in western Canada, M. E. G. Gery. I would like to place before the minister not only my suggestions but those that have come from representative organizations of chartered accountants across this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have them.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
At the present time the employer may deduct a total contribution not to exceed $1,500 of approved schemes; for past services an additional amount regulated by the terms of the approved scheme; and in respect of retirement allowance, a lump sum payment made in the year of retirement. The employee may deduct a percentage, usually 5 per cent of the employee's wage, but in no case exceeding $1,500; and, as far as past services are concerned, an amount not exceeding $1,500 a year in respect to past services when he was not a contributor.
The privilege of tax deferment on the above basis is open only to employees of employers who have arranged for an approved scheme. The result is that many private individuals across Canada are denied an opportunity to follow a similar system

farmers and fishermen, small business concerns operated chiefly by proprietors or partners, professional men practising singly or in groups, and employed persons whose employers have not provided an approved pension scheme.
I feel that something should be done in order to encourage people of this type to do what those under approved pension systems may do, namely purchase now for their security in the future. I believe that a system could be evolved, and I would be prepared to submit to any committee set up for

the purpose a series of suggestions in that regard which would bring about equality with those in approved pension plans for those who do not come within such schemes; so that many people who are now denied the opportunity of doing that which employers and employees under approved schemes are able to do would thereby be encouraged to save and make provision for themselves for the days ahead.
I know one of the criticisms of the plan I suggest, that one type of saving should not be singled out for tax exemption. Well, it is being done now in the case of approved schemes. It is argued that a widespread extension might seriously affect the economy of the country in lowered tax revenues. My answer is that the plan evolved would have to be within restrictions and subject to regulations.
There are others who claim that it would deny expansion in our country, that it would dry up the sources of moneys that are necessary for development purposes. My answer to that argument is that such pension funds would be available to be loaned to industry and the like, in much the same way as loans are made by credit unions. I believe that, if this type of thing were brought into being and extended to the groups I have mentioned, it would be an encouragement to savings, it would pay off dividends in the future, and it would bring about equality which is being denied, when one section of the community is allowed to do this while others are denied the opportunity and the privilege of so doing.
I suggest those four matters for consideration by the government, matters that do not receive any attention to speak of in the budget. I know there are those who say we can soak the rich in this country, and that corporate taxation can be continued indefinitely. I can think of nothing that would encourage greater development today, when it is so necessary and when we face deficit financing, than a very considerable reduction in the amount of corporate taxation and an increase in the personal exemption for income tax purposes.
Look at the record, which reveals how the purchasing power of money has gone down in recent years. Compare 1938 with today. On the basis of 1938 an income of $2,000 has a purchasing power today of $1,103. Present income of $3,000 has a purchasing power of $1,567, and a present income of $4,000 has a purchasing power of $2,020. An income of $6,000 today has a purchasing power of $2,955, in every case after taxes have been paid. That indicates the answer to those who speak of the higher prices the farmer receives
The Budget-Mr. Diefenbaker for his wheat compared with the prices in 1938. The other day the hon. member for Calgary North dealt with that matter and showed that one of the reasons agriculture now finds itself in a difficult position is the fact that the purchasing power of a bushel of wheat is less than it was in 1938.
There is nothing in the budget to indicate a realistic approach to conditions in Canada The government sits in its supremacy. It does not even accept any more the recommendations of its own party friends in convention assembled. When only recently the national executive of the Liberal party recommended something that we of the opposition have suggested over the years, the setting up of an administrative body to govern relations between the C.B.C. and the private stations, the answer given by the Prime Minister the next day, using the words that I had placed before him in the question, was that such a body was not desirable or necessary.
Demands for reductions in taxation have come to the government not only from the opposition groups but also from various Liberal organizations across the country, and the attitude of the government is in effect, "After all, we know what is best." The budget indicates that the government follows the myth of its own self-satisfied perfection which its publicists across Canada so often indicate it possesses, and refuses to act realistically. There is nothing in the budget that will start the wheels of industry turning. There is nothing that will bring back into employment the thousands who are unemployed.
Do we receive any reply from the Prime Minister when we ask him what is to be done for labour and the farmer and industry? What stand are you going to take, what encouragement are you going to hold out to the Canadian people? We have gone through a long budget debate. No minister has yet stated during this debate what is to be done to encourage the expansion of employment in this country. The attitude of the government is the attitude of those who, during the days of private buccaneering in the United States, used to say, "The public be damned". That has been the attitude of this government in these days. We have wondered on occasion why the government resents being criticized. They do resent it.
A few weeks ago Mr. Duncan MacTavish stated in Edmonton at a party meeting that there is no danger in the one-party state as long as the one party contains such fine men as there are in the government now. One can only say that the government did not regard that as eulogy. They regarded it as unadulterated fact. At the national Liberal

The Budget-Mr. Diefenbaker federation meeting, in the accents of dictatorship, he asked himself some questions. What about these opposition members? They speak of unemployment, and they do this in the hope of improving their chances of capturing the federal government. Has it become one of the major sins in a democracy for the opposition to believe that ultimately it will become the alternative government? Then he went on to say:
Mischievous little boys who play with fire and cause public damage can be punished . . . But mischief committed in the guise of free speech... escapes the punishment it deserves . . .
Shades of Mackenzie King, Mr. Speaker! These are the accents of dictatorship. These are the thoughts of those too long in power. They are not only the views of Mr. MacTavish but also the views of the Prime Minister. Recall that he has not disavowed that outrageous doctrine enunciated by the president of the national Liberal federation. In a speech he made on the same occasion the Prime Minister, dealing with the criticism of unemployment, said:
That sort of talk can easily lead to defeatist thinking and can destroy that buoyant confidence which has been so large a factor in building our nation.
Not only did the Prime Minister not disavow what Mr. MacTavish said, he actually adopted it when he himself spoke. These are dangerous views on the part of any government and reveal what happens when governments become all-powerful and remain in power beyond the term that governments ordinarily remain in power. I ask the Prime Minister: Is he going to tell the people of Canada before this debate is over what is going to be done, what plans he has in mind, what hope there is for the unemployed?
The Minister of Finance has his own views on the subject. He has even become saturated with a similar philosophy. He spoke the other day at Toronto and I have his words here. He said-and he can deny it if I misquote him in any way-that he did not believe there was much unemployment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I did not say that.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will find the quotation in a moment. He said he did not believe there was much unemployment because if there was the government would not be as popular as it is. I hope I have the quotation available. It has to do with a speech the minister made in Toronto within the last two or three days on the subject of unemployment, and is taken from the Toronto Star. I had it before but I do not have it at the moment. However, I will certainly see that the minister gets it so that he will be in a position to deny its accuracy. He could not understand that unemployment was as

serious as it had been pictured to be. He could not understand that situation at all. According to the Toronto Daily Star this is what the minister said:
Turning to the federal field Mr. Harris said he did not think unemployment in Canada is as bad as opposition spokesmen say it is.
Opposition spokesmen say so, and so do the bureau of statistics and the employment bureau.
"If it were, if, as the opposition claims, people are really suffering, which I doubt, then I would like to ask the opposition how it is the government retains its popularity."
In other words, instead of admitting the seriousness of the situation as revealed by the bureau of statistics the minister says in effect, "It cannot be because, after all, look at us-a government the epitome of all popularity, the acme of all the perfections." When the people of Canada need a shot in the arm, they receive a scratch on the arm. Then the minister went on to say this:
"I have never known a time when any grievances the people had were not reflected in their opinion of the government of the day."
That is a sorry answer to the unemployed across this country. As to the future, they are simply told that the records may reveal unemployment but so far as we are concerned, look at us; we know what is right and are the personification of' all popularity.
Mr. Calder suggested the need of economy in government; what is being done in that regard? The minister mentioned economies of some $4 million out of non-defence expenditures amounting to some $2 billion. No serious endeavour whatever has been made to meet the situation. One could quote examples, and the opportunity will come when the estimates are being considered.
A few years ago Gladstone, that revered leader of Liberalism, said "Public economy is a public virtue." A mere $4 million cut off such vast expenditures outside of defence and defence production does not indicate that serious regard for economical government that ought to characterize good government. The explanation given by the minister for the reduction in national productive income was the failure of the western wheat crop last year. Trade has disappeared and our wheat exports have been decreasing during the last year. They went down last year, although in the last few weeks there has been some degree of increase over and above last year's corresponding period.
What do we find so far as the farmers are concerned? The Canadian farmer faces one of the most serious challenges to his continuance. His costs are rising and the prices of the things the farmer has to sell are going

down. During the five years between 1949 and 1954 farm costs in Canada increased by 17 per cent; living costs by 13 per cent; and farm prices in general across the board were down by approximately 21-6 per cent. The explanation given for this condition is the failure of the western farmers' wheat crop, and that is nothing but an excuse.
The western farmer suffered a serious crop failure in 1954. The farmers' income in 1954-55 has been maintained through the sale of the wheat and other grain products that were produced earlier. It will not be until this year that we will begin to realize the terrific impact of last year's failure of the western farmers' crop on the Canadian economy. One of the main reasons for the depression in the national income last year was the fact that we lost our markets abroad for wheat. The annual report of the Canadian Pacific Railway which came out in the middle of April so states in regard to the reduction of the traffic volume:
The greater part of the reduction in traffic volume was accounted for by a decrease of about one-third in the movement of grain and grain products because of reduced export demands.
The Regina Leader-Post says this:
The government budget white paper confirms that wheat export difficulties were the major factors in the dislocation of our economy in 1954.
I emphasize those words. It was not a fall-off in farm production in 1954 that caused the farmers' reduced income; but was the result of the government's inability to sell wheat. Grain exports dropped by almost $300 million in 1954, an amount greater than the total decline of all exports in 1954 of $223 million. While exports of motor vehicles, primary iron and steel and defence materials also declined, there were significant offsetting increases in other export categories. I repeat that it was not the failure of the western wheat crop in 1954 that reduced national income; it was not climatic conditions in western Canada in 1954, but it was the failure of this government to take any effective action to assure the preservation of our wheat markets abroad.
As of March 9, according to the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix, 143,900,000 bushels of wheat are stored on Saskatchewan farms. Whenever agriculture suffers and the farmers' income goes down, it immediately disrupts the economy everywhere within the dominion. In 1953 Canadian exports of wheat and wheat flour amounted to 385 million bushels; in 1954, they amounted to 255 million. Because there was no export market there was no sale for the farmers' wheat at the local elevator. During seven months, the period for which I have been able to secure the information, from August to February in 1952-53, there
The Budget-Mr. Richardson were 207-8 million bushels of wheat exported by Canada. In 1953-54 for the same seven-month period the export was 152-7 million bushels. In 1954-55, for the same seven months, the export was 152 million bushels. In other words, the fall-away since 1952-53 in both years for the seven months was approximately 54 million bushels. Canada's carryover on August 1, 1953, was 369-2 million bushels, and on August 1, 1954 it was 582-7 million. So it is all nonsense to explain that the reason for the fall in the national product was in large measure due to the failure of the wheat crop on the prairies last year.
The situation may also be viewed from another angle, a reference to the actual sales of wheat made by farmers between August 1 and April 20 in two succeeding years. Between August 1, 1953, and April 20, 1954, the sales amounted to 270,080,000 bushels while between August 1, 1954 and April 20, 1955 it was 167,490,000. I repeat that in large measure the fall in national income was due to the fact that the western wheat farmer took the rap, through the failure of this government to provide and maintain markets abroad.
Again, I make the appeal I have made on other occasions, for the intensification of the campaign to sell our wheat in the markets of the world. How is this to be done? That is a problem, a tremendous problem; but it is worthy of note that when in 1950 and 1951 this party made motions in the house to the effect that there should be convened British commonwealth trade conferences, and pointed out the danger to the markets of Canadian farmers in respect of wheat and other grains, each and every member supporting the government ridiculed the suggestion and voted down the motions. I believe one thing that could be done even now, with Australia, the United States and the Argentine securing a larger share of the world wheat market than they secured proportionately three years ago, would be for Canada to begin now to place in each of our embassies-and they are spread all over the world-agricultural market representatives whose duties would be the intensification of a campaign for the sale of our wheat.
Sir, my time has expired, and I will now conclude.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is only proper that, at the outset, I should speak in the language of the majority of the people of the province of Quebec, being one of its representatives, for it is the language of people who have had such a glorious part in the development of this country.
3618	HOUSE OF COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Richardson
As you are aware, Mr. Speaker, I was born in Acadia, in that region now known as the province of Nova Scotia, a fact of which I am proud. I have however chosen to live in the province of Quebec, where I have been residing over the past 30 years.
My French being far from excellent, my colleagues-those from this side of the house at least-will no doubt allow me to continue my remarks in my native tongue.
(Text):
Mr. Speaker, there are few observations of real value that a member entering this chamber for the first time can probably make. Your new member for St. Lawrence-St. George has made a solemn pledge with himself that certainly, for at least one session-this session- that member shall not use up the 40-minute allotment, but shall restrict himself, as well as he can, within, say, 15 or 20 minutes. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, when hon. members opposite see the hands of the clock approaching 20 minutes after four I ask that they call "time" upon this speaker.
The member for St. Lawrence-St. George is essentially and basically a man of peace, but he suggests that on this sunny afternoon we declare war. Now, I do not mean by that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) should enter the chamber and state solemnly that no longer are we at peace with a certain country. But, with greatest respect, sir, and fellow members, following the example set by the government on many occasions, could we not, man for man and regardless of party, renew our declaration of war upon waste of human personality in Canada, waste of effort, waste of our great natural resources and, without wishing to show any disrespect to hon. members to whom I have listened for four months-and, may I say, with great profit to myself-waste of time.
Without any desire to transgress the rule I have laid down for myself, and not wishing to waste even one of the 20 minutes I have allotted to myself, on some future occasion I should like to pay my respects and the respects of the constituency of St. Lawrence-St. George to at least three of my predecessors- those since 1921. I refer first to the distinguished Sir Herbert Marler, the great brother of a distinguished member of the present cabinet. Then there comes to my mind a name which, when uttered, may cause some of my confreres on this side to shudder -that great and distinguished giant, Charles Cahan who, in the traditions of his party and according to his lights, at his particular time made, as did Sir Herbert Marler, and other predecessors, great contributions in this

chamber. Last but not least-because only too recently has he moved from the public scene-the man who in this chamber from the dread days of 1944 on to 1954 administered with relentless devotion not one department but two great departments. You all know his name, because it is a simple one: Brooke Claxton.
In any forum of debate in which human beings congregate we all, perhaps with some rare exceptions-and they may be on the other side, where it may be alleged there is the greater degree of intelligence-make mistakes in our terms. May I at the outset pay my respects to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) because, listening to him a good deal, I have concluded that he is a great repository of information. We recall that when the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) was making that informative address about a week ago, the hon. member interjected, "Are your figures in constant dollars?"
How frequently in all forms of debate, not only in the House of Commons but throughout Canada, do we fail to compare dollar with dollar when we begin making comparisons in modern life. We also frequently fail to recognize the significance of the terms we use- and nowhere more frequently than in this very chamber. For instance, not always do we recognize what you and I and our fellow citizens mean by the word "government". While in the technical sense we know what a government or a cabinet is, many of us, while we walk on the street, read our newspapers or chat with our friends, fail to realize that when we ask the government to make expenditures it means that somebody somewhere in Canada has to pay a price, and usually vast numbers of us do.
Again, and I shall not go on for long because I want to be well within my limited time, the term "wealth" is used so frequently that people believe one can stretch into the air and pull down currency or gold. But wealth, after all, is a very simple thing to understand. It is human work or productivity, mechanical or other forms of power, applied to natural resources.
In the ambit of just those few terms may I, Mr. Speaker, with some temerity as a freshman in this house, now relate my remarks to four speakers on the opposite side? I refer first of all, with great respect, to a friend and colleague of long standing, the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Mac-donnell). I regret that he is not here at this time. I wish he were so that I could direct

my remarks to him. face to face. He said, as reported at page 2947 of Hansard:
You may be able to do it on budget night and get away with it. but it catches up with you.
Later on he said:
The press is catching up. It is interesting to note that a loyal, stout-hearted supporter of the government-I think I am describing them correctly-the Toronto Star, ignores the minister's exhilaration and evidently feels, indeed it calls, the *outlook uncertain.
Then he quotes the Toronto Star as follows:
"Mr. Harris' maiden speech will come as a disappointment to the many Canadians who hoped it would stimulate production and reduce unemployment."
I continue to quote, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member for Greenwood said:
I continue to read from the Star: "Taken as a whole it is really an unimaginative stand-pat budget that in itself will provide little relief from our present economic problem.
The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George has almost within the confines of his constituency two great papers, perhaps some would say not as great as those which are published in another large metropolitan city of Canada, but they are very good papers. One of them is the Montreal Gazette which has, if I correctly observe Canadian history, never been known to be tremendously *enthusiastic over the people who now sit on this side of you, Mr. Speaker. As a matter of fact, I rather think, if my political history is right, that the destinies of that great paper for many years were presided over by Mr. Robert Smeaton White, who was a venerable member of another political party in this house.
May I digress for a moment to say that the editor of the Montreal Gazette long adorned our press gallery. I refer to Mr. John Bassett. When I met one of his associates a day or two after the election-Mr. Bassett happens to be one of my neighbours and constituents -he asked me how I liked the editorial that had appeared two or three days before November 8, which made very kind reference to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) and myself. I said:	"If my friend, now the
Minister of Transport, and the present member for St. Lawrence-St. George, had died and passed to their fathers on November 8, we should have got, I suspect, a much longer obituary in your Montreal Gazette than we did in your editorial, but it was very kind and very helpful."
This is the editorial from the Montreal Gazette of April 6, the heading is:
Easing the Burden
Hon. Walter Harris has decided to use tailing taxes as a weapon with which to fight falling revenues. It is a courageous course.
The Budget-Mr. Richardson
Particularly notable in last night's budget was the decision to cut corporation taxes.
This is an important decision, for it shows a sound perception of the role of corporations as the foundation of Canada's prosperity.
I now come to the end of the editorial:
But the important thing is that Mr. Harris has shown a readiness to count upon Canadians, in their business and as persons, to take a hand in improving their own future, and he has made some leeway in government tax demands to enable them to do so. This is a far sounder approach than to try to improve conditions by still more government activity and a still more entangled tax jungle.
The losses that the government will take in its revenues, as a result of the tax cuts, are regarded by Mr. Harris as a calculated investment in the country's future. The economic lift they will give the economy may, in due course, produce new sources of revenue, by broadening the base.
This is, surely, the right approach. And surely it comes at the right time.
May I now turn to another section of the chamber. Again I regret that the hon. member is not present, not that he would gain much from my remarks, but I fail to see the leader of the party of which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is a supporter. I refer to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). As I read the debates of last year I find that he made a mistake in a tax observation, and he repeated, and made doubly bad, this year that very same mistake. May I, with all due deference to a member who has great intelligence, a great heart and great personal integrity, I am sure, say that he failed to tell the whole truth in this chamber when he dealt with this particular subject. I should like to refer to page 2957 of Hansard. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, in dealing with the dividend credit said:
In 1949 the tax credit allowed receivers of dividends from Canadian corporations was first introduced. In 1953 this tax credit was increased to 20 per cent producing, as I pointed out at the time, the fantastic result that a married man with no children who received all his income from clipping coupons could receive up to $9,760 free of personal income tax. That was the position in the 1954 taxation year.
Then he went on to say that as a result of the changes this year the minister will have increased the $9,760 free of income tax to $11,133.33, which the coupon clipper may receive in dividends before paying any personal income tax. I particularly note the use of the word "personal"; but may I suggest that some people throughout Canada, and in fact some members of this house, may be under the impression that from a tax point of view that is the whole story. I submit, Mr. Speaker, it is not. 1 shall try to demonstrate that in a few sentences.
At the bottom of page 2957 of Hansard the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar gave

The Budget-Mr. Richardson a table and he assumed that this particular taxpayer to whom he referred had unearned income of approximately $11,000. Now, there is exactly where certain terms that I referred to earlier are misunderstood. Certainly, Mr. Speaker, my fellow colleagues of the bar will join me when I say that a corporation is a legal fiction; it is an artificial creation. But to create the wealth, the goods or the profits which a corporation must produce you must have men and individuals to do so.
Let me make the case extreme. Assume that the company is owned by one individual. Before that individual gets this unearned income, being dividends of approximately $11,000, there must be net profits of the company, and before there are any net profits there must be gross profits. It is relatively simple so far. But the profits, after certain deductions if you like, are shared, as every member of this house should know, by the taxpayers of Canada, sometimes called the government. Up to now all other taxpayers shared in those profits to the extent of 49 per cent, leaving this one individual who owned the company, who gave forth his efforts in establishing the corporation, to get the remainder of the net profits, 51 per cent. So in order to produce approximately $11,000 of dividends this individual had to have his corporation earn profits of $21,830, of which his fellow Canadian taxpayers got $10,696. That is the amount which our friend the shareholder had to pay indirectly, through the corporation, to his fellow taxpayers of Canada.
The example given by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar would have been more appropriate if under his heading of coupon clippers instead of "none" as the tax paid by him, the member had shown this $10,696 as a comparable figure. Mind you, no man in this chamber will stand up and say that I am on the side of the coupon clippers only rather than of all those who make the real wealth of the country. The member for St. Lawrence-St. George has justified his own living by good, hard manual work. I do not share in the criticism, and I will stop it in advance, from anyone who says this example is given to protect the coupon clipper.
This coupon clipper pays to his fellow taxpayers, through the government, $10,696, whereas the salaried worker or the wage earner pays, as the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar has well said, $1,817. Our friend who is the shareholder of the corporation pays approximately six times as much after assuming the risk of losses as well as profits, after establishing the company with initiative and pioneering spirit, and engaging the salaried man and other wage earners.

speechtext: The hon. member has had 20 minutes. The hon. member asked us to call his attention to the time.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Thank you very much. I shall sit down in just a moment. I know I have had 20 minutes but I will stop in just a minute. The May 5 issue of Financial Counsel published in Toronto and Montreal had this headline:
T.V. Boom Continues to Roar Ahead.
The booming industry of manufacturing television sets shows no signs of slowing down despite the hectic pace of expansion in recent years. In the first quarter of 1955, a new sales record of 116,462 sets valued at $51,419,791 was established.
Then on page 3 of the same issue we find an item stating that Canadian International
The Budget-Mr. Richardson
Paper Company is to erect a $2 million plant, and the paragraph continues:
Another step in the capital expenditure program of Canadian International Paper Company will soon be taken when a start is made in the near future on a $2,000,000 plant at Pointe Aux Trembles, Quebec, just east of Montreal. This new plant will produce special containers and will employ several hundred people when it has reached the final stage, according to latest reports.
And again:
Present building program involves an increase in pulping capacity and installation of the world's largest machine for making kraft liner board at La Tuque.
Mr. Speaker, I shall finish now if you will allow me just one minute of my remaining 18 minutes' time.
The budget is of course a report to the shareholders of Canada, who are all taxpayers including ourselves. I have two suggestions. One is a relatively simple and inexpensive way to let all of us taxpayers know exactly what we are paying in the way of income tax and for what purpose. On the reverse of the assessment notice which goes out to all of our four million taxpayers in Canada there could, without any great expense in printing, be put the seven major items of expenditure; defence, welfare and pensions program, public debt charges, provincial payments, resources and industrial development, national overhead and miscellaneous. Against those seven descriptions there could be placed the exact amounts that are spent. Another column could show precisely the percentage, for example, about 40 per cent for national defence.
There could be another-the last-column on the right where any taxpayer, even those who are in this chamber, with a pencil, may relate his percentage which is to be paid for national defence. If it is estimated at 40 per cent, the taxpayer will know that out of his total tax bill of $1,000, $400 will be spent on his behalf for defence. That is a relatively cheap price at the moment to pay for security within Canada. Each taxpayer will know precisely what his share of the income tax burden is with regard to national welfare benefits, with regard to the debt charges and other features of our national administration.
Although at first glance this may seem a little strange, many taxpayers in Canada are anxious to have-and certainly need-information of this character. I do not believe we have any interest in prolonging the debate here, but my own view is that we should inform the taxpayers who are our shareholders. speechtext:
In regard to the budget, it is interesting to note that from 1945 to 1953 we had in this country generally a sellers' market, bringing an expansion in both production and income. The job of the Minister of Finance during that period was comparatively easy. The economy was forging ahead, and it was only necessary for the minister to apply the brakes from time to time. Today the economy has slowed down and there is a very definite need to push sales in order to maintain the expansion in both production and income.
I would say that the present period provides the first real test of the government's ability to maintain an expansion of production in the face of somewhat adverse conditions. One might say that today the home market has been very definitely neglected.
I think the Minister of Finance will agree that the home market is the best market we have, because it has to absorb an amount of goods equivalent to the total production of the country. I would also say it is the best market, because it is the only market over which we have absolute control. But it has been sorely neglected in the past, and it can be argued that it is being neglected today.
Certainly we have in Canada today a tremendous potential market consisting of the people receiving low incomes. The minister stressed the sustaining force of welfare


payments. I think the minister will agree that those payments could be still further expanded without laying themselves open to the charge of extravagance. Expanding those payments would strengthen their sustaining force in so far as the economy is concerned.
I regret that the Minister of Finance did not see fit to reduce the sales tax, which would have helped to expand the purchasing power of those people who are in greatest need of having their purchasing power expanded. It would also have helped to expand sales by reducing the prices of commodities, and that would have been of special value in the international market, because we are constantly being told that our prices are not competitive.
In his address the minister blamed the short wheat crop for the decline in the Canadian economy. Obviously that cannot be the case. By the end of 1954 we had not even sold the 1953 crop. If we should happen to have another crop failure this year I think the government will realize the seriousness of the situation because, having had a crop failure last year, another crop failure this year would bring about a drop in farm income which would be exceptionally serious.
What the minister should have said was that the decline in the Canadian economy was due largely to the drop in the farmers' income. Agriculture today is undoubtedly facing very difficult times, owing to falling prices, the difficulty in selling farm produce, and adverse weather conditions.
The bureau of statistics, in its publication "Farm Net Income, 1954", demonstrates the effect of these conditions. It is important to note that the figures I am quoting are of net income. Whenever you refer to the situation with regard to agriculture you should always use the net income figures rather than gross income, because gross income in itself has little significance. You must take into consideration the cost involved and what is left afterward. That is the income the farmer has left to spend.
In 1951 the net income of the farmers was $2,154 million; in 1952, $1,923-5 million; in 1953, $1,699-6 million; in 1954, $1,125-6 million, a drop of over $1 billion in four years. So we find today that the farmers, representing approximately 16 per cent of the population, are only receiving 6 per cent of the national income. The whole economy is suffering as a result. I think the minister would agree that everything that can possibly be done to halt that downward trend must be done. It is not merely the farmers who will suffer; the whole Canadian economy will suffer as a consequence.

We believe three things are essential in order to strengthen the agricultural situation. We believe the price support program should be strengthened. We believe definite action should be taken to expand markets for agricultural produce both at home and abroad. We believe the government should take the initiative in establishing a crop insurance program in co-operation with the provinces.
I am only going to deal with the question of support prices at this time. I shall be dealing with the other two matters at some other time, probably on the agriculture estimates. However, before going on with this matter I wish to refer to a statement made by the hon. member for Assiniboia when he spoke in this debate. He stated that the C.C.F. was the only party in Canada advocating that support prices should be at full parity, that is parity prices supported rigidly on that basis. I would point out that it is true they are the only political party, so far as I know, advocating that policy; but it is also interesting to note that none of the major farm organizations is advocating that support prices should be maintained at 100 per cent of parity. If there is any doubt on that point, perhaps I should quote from the brief of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture.
It is also interesting to note that when the hon. member for Assiniboia spoke he referred to the brief of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture as a very excellent brief. This is what they have to say regarding the proposal of the C.C.F. to maintain support prices at 100 per cent of parity, as found at page 7 of their brief:
We do not believe it is sound or practical to look to a price support program to guarantee the farmer prices which represent a full fair or parity relationship for each individual product. The result of such 100 per cent guarantees, if attempted, would inevitably be a high degree of government direction and control over agriculture. We do not believe farmers wish to submit to such extensive government participation in their business, nor do we believe it is reasonable to ask the government to undertake such a commitment. We believe that a parity position for agriculture can be achieved not only through a clearly defined price support program, but through the development of producer orderly marketing programs and the full co-operation of governments in all essential features of sound farm, economic and trade policy.
It is interesting to note that in their brief the Canadian Federation of Agriculture advocates partially flexible support prices being maintained at between 65 and 85 per cent of parity. The hon. member for Assiniboia says their brief is very excellent, so apparently he is in favour of maintaining support prices
The Budget-Mr. Quelch at not more than 85 per cent of parity. On the other hand, in his own speech he advocated 100 per cent of parity.

The hon. member for Assiniboia went out of his way to criticize what the leader of this group had had to say regarding parity prices. If it had not been for that I probably would not have mentioned the subject at all. At page 3459 of Hansard the hon. member had this to say:
In his opening speech this session the leader of the Social Credit party had some remarks to make about parity prices. He said that his party was in favour of flexible parity prices, in other words, prices that were only a percentage of parity and which did not give the farmer the full equitable treatment he deserves.
Let me say that statement is absolutely false. I am not suggesting it was deliberately made as false; nevertheless it is an absolutely untrue statement. Unfortunately I think the hon. member for Assiniboia has allowed his political astuteness to pervert his mind in this regard. The trouble with the hon. member for Assiniboia is that he apparently does not understand the meaning of the word "flexible". He takes it for granted that the word "flexible" means less, but of course it can mean more or less, above parity or below parity. If it were considered desirable to expand the production of any one commodity and reduce the production of another, then it might be considered desirable to increase the support price above parity on the commodity you wanted to expand and decrease it on the other. There is no indication that by flexible support prices the leader of this group meant price supports below parity. Then the hon. member for Assiniboia went on to say:
In case the hon. member may think I am misrepresenting what he said-
Let me point out there is no doubt about that.
-I shall quote his exact words as reported on page 47 of Hansard for January 10, 1955:
"There is a very good case that can be made in favour of the adoption of such a flexible system here in Canada, the percentage of parity that is used of course to depend upon the amount of incentive which ought to be provided to achieve the amount of production that is required to meet the need.''
That is the statement on which he bases his contention that we were advocating less than parity and an inequitable treatment of the farmers. If he had gone on a little further he could not possibly have fallen under that delusion. Let me quote from the same page

The Budget-Mr. Quelch he quoted from as to what the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) stated:
The problem we face In this country is to adopt some policy and some technique which will guarantee the farmers their fair share of the national income. The figures will bear out what I say. The farmers who make up approximately 20 per cent of the population of Canada, received in 1953 only 99 per cent of the national income . . .
I say the problem to be faced in a country like Canada is to adopt a policy which will guarantee the farmers a fair share of the national income. It would be only just and right if the farmers as a class make up 20 per cent of the total population of our country, they should receive something like 20 per cent of the national income. There has hardly been a time in the history of this country when this has been the case.
To achieve that, we advocate flexible parity prices based upon a two-price system, and I will be dealing with that later in my remarks. I think that is all I need to say to clarify the situation regarding the charge of the member for Assiniboia that we are advocating parity prices of an inequitable nature. He did suggest to me that I should straighten that out when I spoke.

speechtext:
There are a number of points that are generally raised in connection with the subject of parity prices. If you are speaking to people down east about western agriculture they will invariably say, "What right have the farmers of Canada to expect the government to underwrite their prices?" I think it is quite a reasonable question. To answer it you have to go back a number of years. You have to go back to the depression years before the war, when farm prices were at a very low level, far below parity. When the farm organizations protested about the low prices they were told that the cause was the international situation, that prices were low in the world market and the farmers could not very well expect to get more than the prices in the world market. So prices continued at a low level in those pre-war years.
Then the war came and within a couple of years the prices of farm products started to rise, but the government considered it desirable to place a ceiling on those prices. Let me point out that you cannot have it both ways. If you say the farmers should take low prices when world prices are low, then surely the farmers are entitled to high prices when world prices are high. But they were not allowed to have those high world prices. Ceilings were placed on them at the very time when the farmers had an opportunity to make up the losses they suffered when prices were so low in the depression years.

The government of the day apparently realized the situation was not fair so far as agriculture was concerned, and the prime minister of the day, Right Hon. Mackenzie King, had this to say in a radio broadcast on December 4, 1943:
I wish tonight to thank the farmers of Canada for their magnificent contribution to the battle of production. I wish again to appeal to them to continue to help hold the front line against inflation by continuing to support the price ceiling. If, to help win the war, the farmers are asked to accept a ceiling on prices, we believe they are entitled to a floor under prices to ensure them against an agricultural depression after the war. As an essential part of its post-war policy, the government intends to ask parliament at the next session to place a floor under the prices of main farm commodities.
The government lived up to that promise and instituted the Agricultural Prices Support Act. Under that act the principle was established that prices for farm products should be maintained at a level that bears a fair relationship to the prices of other commodities. The question, of course, that is in the minds of many farmers is whether the government today is living up to that principle.
I was interested in that point. I was wondering whether the support prices of farm products today were in line with the principle laid down under the Agricultural Prices Support Act, so I wrote the chairman of the agricultural prices support board. On a former occasion I had written to the bureau of statistics but the Minister of Agriculture told me I had written to the wrong body, and I should have written to the agricultural prices support board. This time, therefore, I wrote to the board. The letter was as follows:
Dear Mr. Shaw:
Could you please send me a list of the commodities that are being supported today and the level of the support price.
In addition, could you also give me what the price of these products would be if the price of farm products today bore the same relationship to the prices of other commodities as existed in the base years 1943-44-45.
I would like to get that information on cattle, as well as hogs, eggs, cheese and butter.
I received a very courteous reply from the agricultural prices support board, and I will just quote the last three paragraphs. They read as follows:
In connection with the second paragraph of your letter I am not quite certain as to the interpretation but I assume you are referring to the basis of relationship mentioned in subsection (2) of section 9 of the Agricultural Prices Support Act which states:
"The board shall endeavour to ensure adequate and stable returns for agriculture by promoting orderly adjustment . . . and shall endeavour to secure a fair relationship between the returns from agriculture and those from other producers.''

In order to illustrate the relationship on the basis of the five commodities which you mention the following table shows the position of each commodity mentioned as well as indicating the United States prices which, while not exactly comparable may be used as guides to prices in that country. The United States market prices for the last four years have been included as a basis of comparison. You will also be aware that eggs and butter have been under price support continuously for several years.
I might mention that I did not ask for the prices in the United States, but I can quite understand that he was anxious to put in a
