subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR FAIR ALLOCATION OF BOX CARS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Tuesday when we were discussing this bill I was interrupted at six o'clock. Since then I have had the opportunity to read the speech made on that occasion by the sponsor of the bill, the hon. member for Assiniboia, and in the few minutes left at my disposal I should like to refer briefly to one statement he made.
First of all let me say that I was struck, when reading his speech, by the number of times the word "arbitrary" appears in it. It seems that the hon. member was carried away by his eloquence in the course of the discussion.
I wish to refer more particularly to the statement which appears on page 3412 of Hansard, and to quote the last sentence of the second paragraph and the last sentences of the third paragraph. In referring to the action of the government, the hon. member said the government-
__has permitted the transport controller to
step in and block the farmers' action by cancelling the car order book.

The same thing is repeated in the third paragraph in different words, as follows: Apparently there is no one in the board of grain commissioners or in the ranks of the cabinet who wishes to restore to the farmers this fundamental right. They would far rather continue this conspiracy to deprive the farmers of a fundamental Canadian right.
The hon. member went as far as he could without being unparliamentary, because there are certainly imputations of improper motives here. The suggestion that the controller or the government deliberately set out to deprive the farmer of a fundamental right is, of course, nonsense in this instance.
This takes us back to the time when the car order book was suspended. It would be well to put on the record the facts of that particular case. Surely the hon. member for Assiniboia knows very well what were the reasons for the suspension of the car order book at the time. They were certainly not the reasons suggested in these two paragraphs. At that time, as we all know, there was a demand for a particular grade of grain, a grade other than the prevailing grade of grain that was produced in that area.
The result was that the Canadian wheat board found themselves in a difficult position because they were unable to obtain, or could not readily get, the particular grade for which they had sales. Therefore they had to issue special shipping orders to get that particular grade wherever it was available. Consequently, under conditions such as these the car order book was very difficult to operate.
I believe the controller suspended the car order book at the request of the Canadian wheat board. At any rate, at that time everybody agreed that it was the logical thing to do and it was done by the controller in order to fill the orders the board was getting for the sale of that grade of grain.
Surely everybody still agrees that it was wise for the wheat board to try to sell as much grain as possible. These were the only reasons the car order book was suspended. Last year, as the situation changed, the pools were the most insistent on having the car order book reinstated.
As we all know, the minister suggested last year that the car order book be reinstated, and it was reinstated. I understand that after a year's experience with it the pools are contemplating requesting that it be suspended again. The suggestion that the transport controller, or any other agency, and the cabinet ministers had purposely set out to prevent the farmers from getting box cars through the car order book is simply ridiculous. It is not a fair statement to make.



Again and again in his speech the hon. member referred to the government directly or indirectly denying to the farmer the right to deliver to the elevator of his choice. He even went so far as to suggest that in this instance the government had taken away the right of the farmer. Earlier in his remarks- and this is what I want to refer to before I conclude-he proceeded to give advice to the people of eastern Canada on this question of box car distribution. I think I should reread for the record the remarks of the hon. member, since he is a member of the socialist group. He said, at page 3411 of Hansard:
The right is that any Canadian, when he decides to sell his produce-whether it be agricultural produce or whether it be his labour-has a right to sell that product to the firm of his own choosing. To say that western farmers today have that freedom would be to deny the truth of the statements by thousands of farmers that have been received by members of parliament and by the government.
We know that other people of whom the hon. member spoke in a derogatory way later on in his speech have been using this very statement in their publicity. Apparently everybody agrees on that, but if the purpose here is to clarify the situation for the eastern members, we might as well state the facts exactly as they are.
As far as the selling of our products is concerned, a few years ago we all agreed and I think we still agree-or at least a very large majority of the farmers of western Canada agreed-that they would forgo the right to sell to any particular firm. By instituting the Canadian wheat board we agreed to let that board be the sole agency to buy our products, and we retained the right to choose the firm to handle our grain. We all have the same right today. It has not been denied to anybody; it has not been taken away by anybody. The situation today is that in some instances we find that the exercise of this right has been curtailed to some degree. It has been curtailed in varying degrees, depending on the area and the place. For quite a few years it has never been possible to exercise that right in full, because no matter what we do, what distribution we make or what scheme we have, in a centre where there is only one elevator the farmers cannot have the right until that situation changes. Therefore, in effect, no matter what anybody does, this right will be curtailed and has been curtailed to some degree.
If there are enough box cars we all have the right to deliver to the elevator of our choice. If there is more than one elevator in a centre we may have that right again. But, I repeat, if there is only one elevator we have not the choice because, under the quota system, it has not been possible to devise a means by

As I said, we have been circularized and presented with another suggestion by the Saskatchewan wheat pool. It is suggested that this matter go before the agriculture committee. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Assiniboia upon bringing this measure before the house again, because it is of vital importance to the grain growers of western Canada, especially so long as the quota system continues. On previous occasions we have always supported similar amendments, and we shall do so at this time because we believe the farmer should have the right to deliver grain to the elevator of his own choice.
The hon. member for Provencher pointed out that the farmer never had that full right, and he gave as an example that there might be only one elevator at a certain point. That might be true in a particular case, but we know there is more than one elevator at the majority of points in western Canada. Simply because there might be only one elevator at one point should not deny the farmer the right to deliver grain to the elevator of his own choice.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR FAIR ALLOCATION OF BOX CARS
speechtext: I am sure the hon. member does not want to misinterpret what I said. I was not using that as an argument against any of the schemes, but simply to indicate that a full choice was not always available.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR FAIR ALLOCATION OF BOX CARS
speechtext:
I quite understand that the hon. member was not presenting it as an argument, but I assume he was considering it as a factor in the case or he would not have mentioned it. He must have had some reason for doing so.

Canada Grain Act
The principle of this amendment has been endorsed by all the major farm organizations in western Canada such as the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the interprovincial farm union and the three western pools. We support it on the ground that the farmer should have the right to deliver grain to the elevator of his own choice at the time a quota is established.
Second, this would help to restore competition in the purchase of grain by elevator agents. Many of us who have had experience in the marketing of grain in western Canada know that at times the popular elevator will be plugged and if a farmer wishes to market his grain he must take it to one of the other elevators. I know it will be argued that all farmers will be treated in the same way, but that is not quite the case. We know that all elevators look after their special patrons. If an elevator should be plugged and a car is available, the agent will phone his special patrons and tell them to bring in some wheat. Those farmers will load up two or three trucks and bring them in and by the time the other farmers hear about it the space is gone. I am not blaming the farmers for that situation, nor do I blame the elevator agents; it is just a situation that exists.
The whole problem arises from the fact that cars are allocated on the basis of one car per elevator. I know it has been argued that this is not a fact, and it may not always be true; but so far as I know that is the general practice. I have been told that it is the general practice at a number of points. This practice is not followed as far as manufacturing establishments are concerned. The factory with the large production will get the greater number of cars; but in the case of grain elevators, no matter how much wheat farmers may want to take to a specific elevator they all get the same number of cars. This is the result of a state of congestion. As a result of this practice farmers are forced to take wheat to elevators other than those of their own choice if they desire to market their grain.
This amendment would help to restore competition. At the present time there is little if any competition because an agent knows quite well that the grain will come to him when the other elevators are full. Consequently he is free to undergrade, underweigh and overdock because he knows he is going to get the grain in the long run. Farmers are quite often forced to haul their grain to a particular elevator even though they do not like the way it will be handled.
No doubt this is one reason the overages in country elevators are so large. Some
'Mr. Quelch.]
people may say the pool elevators also have overages. This is true, but the farmer knows that if he hauls his wheat to a pool elevator and there are overages he will get the benefit of those through patronage dividends at a later date. That is why so many farmers are anxious to haul their grain to pool elevators. They are not satisfied with the way their grain is being handled by the other elevators. If they haul to a pool elevator they will benefit from any overgrading or underweighing that may take place when the final settlement is made.
If this amendment carries, cars will be allocated to elevators in keeping with the farmers' individual expressed preference. The railways say they are quite willing to do this and are merely waiting for direction from some source. The wheat pools have suggested a somewhat different procedure through an amendment to the wheat board act and the grain act. I am not at all certain in my own mind whether this amendment or the amendments suggested by the wheat pools would be best, but I think we could all agree on the principle of this bill, that the farmer should have the right to deliver his grain to the elevator of his choice.
It seems to me the best thing the house could do would be to approve the principle of this bill on second reading and then send it to the agriculture committee, where it could be amended in line with the best interests of the farmers without changing the principle. We would be able to bring down representatives from the pools and other farm organizations and try to whip this amendment into the best possible form.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR FAIR ALLOCATION OF BOX CARS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to support Bill No. 22 I want first to comment upon the fact that the hon. member for Provencher has said repeatedly that we ought to let this matter stand for a little while longer until we see what the committee is going to do about it. I suggest to him that the wrongs and injustices which have existed in this field have been allowed to go on too long. This bill should have been passed three years ago, and the right of the farmer to deliver grain to the elevator' of his own choice established.
When you take that right away from him you stir him very deeply, particularly when the elevator which he has built represents years of struggle and sacrifice, education and fight. We do not want to go back to the old days when the Winnipeg grain exchange controlled the price of grain when purchased from the farmer and the price at which it was sold to the ultimate consumer or to other

parts of the trade, and then pocketed the difference. As stated in the explanatory note:
The purpose of this act is to remove discrimination in the allocation of box cars by providing in a new section of the car order book a rule for the fair allocation of box cars among elevator companies at a marketing point where the car order book, as presently constituted, is not in effect.
By allocating their seeded acreage among the elevator companies at a marketing point, producers themselves will determine the distribution of box cars at that point.
Many people are somewhat at a loss to understand why there should be so much noise about the right of a farmer to deliver his grain to the elevator of his choice as, after all, he is selling it to the wheat board, and the wheat board is the sole agency to handle it. But there is more than that involved in this. The farmer, in continuing the fight he has carried on for some 30 or 40 years, has established this elevator system to which he wants to deliver. He has been delivering his grain to his elevator for many years. It is part of his life; it is part of his struggle; it represents years of work. He sees a tremendous injustice when box cars are allocated to the elevators at that particular point, and he finds when he wants to deliver grain to his own elevator that there is no room. Why is there no room? Because somebody, in spotting the cars that came in, spotted the cars in front of the other elevators.
The effects of the situation are shown clearly in the annual figures of the Saskatchewan wheat pool, which is the one mostly affected in the past. They found that the annual percentage of business which they have been able to do has gradually fallen off until this year the figure is below 40 per cent. The hon. member for Provencher this afternoon made the point that if you have a siding with only one elevator you have no choice. That is true, but this is what has aggravated the farmer. He finds that if it is a siding with one line elevator that is where he and the farmers in that district deliver their grain. Eight miles further down the line there may be another siding with another elevator, but in this case it is the wheat pool elevator, his own elevator. He finds that the cars are not spotted at the elevators in the right proportions. Sometimes there are two or three times as many cars going to the line elevator company as to the point where there is only the wheat pool elevator.
After they have taken out all the allocated grain which is under quota for that line elevator point, the farmers throughout the country cannot make further delivery. Then suddenly this point is opened up and farmers are allowed to deliver where there is only
Canada Grain Act
one elevator, and that is a line elevator. The result is that farmers are unable to sell the grain. They are short of money. They cannot deliver the grain because no box cars have been delivered at their point. They have no cash and they cannot pay their taxes. Finally in desperation the farmers are forced to deliver the grain to the line elevator company.
Figures show that gradually, in the last four or five years, this business has gone from the wheat pool. The percentage going to the line elevator companies is increasing. They are gaining in strength. These companies were the foundation and the basis of the old Winnipeg grain exchange. This stirs up within the farmers the fear that perhaps the wheat board will be thrown out when the big line companies get strong enough again, when they are handling a large enough quantity of grain that they will be able to re-establish the grain exchange.
The farmers are afraid that the wheat board will be done away with and that, after fighting for 50 years, they will be left to the mercy of the line elevator companies and the grain exchange. This is a battle that has been going on for many years, and the farmer will fight desperately to keep himself out of the clutches of the line elevator companies.
When the wheat pool first started, years ago, the line elevator companies tried to meet their competition but were unable to do so. The wheat pool has grown over the years. In the province of Saskatchewan over 1,100 co-operative wheat pool elevators are handling the business for co-operative farmers. Now they find they are unable to deliver their grain there.
Something must have prevented them from doing so, and it was not competition. They beat the line elevator companies in competition every time they met, and they drove the line elevator companies out of business at many points by doing business better and by returning to the farmers the profits of their organization. The farmer got his profits on the grain he delivered there in proportion to the business he did. But somehow, through machinations in the allocation of box cars- this is the weapon which the opposition to the wheat pool has used-the pool elevators find themselves strangled.
We have been trying to find out who was responsible for the allocation of box cars. The transport controller denies that he is responsible. The railway companies say that they do not get any instructions from anybody, and it is simply that freight crews go down and happen to leave a box car at one place or another. They may say all the

Canada Grain Act
elevators are filled and so, if there are four cars, they will send one to each elevator. That means that the farmers' co-operative is only getting 25 per cent of the business and that is all it can get. Perhaps 75 or 80 per cent of the farmers have been delivering their grain to that point. They want to deliver their grain to their own elevator but they have to haul it to the line elevator companies.
Those in control of the line elevator companies have exploited the farmers. When the farmer is forced to deliver his grain to the line elevator companies, the agent will say, "We will give you a good grade on this. I think you had better bring your permit book here, so we will handle all your grain." A regular battle has gone on for some time to win over the farmer.
We can easily understand why the Winnipeg grain exchange wants to get back into business. If they can handle the farmers' grain again and manipulate prices to suit themselves the farmer will have to take the price offered him. They will be permitted to manipulate the price and nobody will be interfering with the principle of private enterprise. They say that the law of supply and demand will be operating again. The wheat pools and the wheat board will be out of the way. The statement of the president of the Winnipeg grain exchange in the past year showed very clearly that what he is aiming at is to restore the line elevator companies and bring back the open market set-up that existed before.
The farmer is alive to that. The chief obstacle to the old grain exchange is the cooperative wheat pool and the Canadian wheat board. The farmers see in this serious behind the scenes set up, where nobody seems to understand the basis upon which the allocation of box cars is made, a sinister move to destroy their organization. That is why they are aroused. That is why they are putting in their protests.
I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce knows that thousands of letters of protest have come from the farmers of Saskatchewan. At any rate hundreds have come to the desks of members of parliament, urging them to support a bill which will give the farmer the right to deliver his grain to whatever elevator he wishes. If he wants to deliver his grain to his own elevator he should be allowed to do so, because it can easily be done. It could be based upon the seeded acreage which each farmer has in the district. It could be arranged in such proportions that each permit holder would tell the station agent at that point exactly the acreage he is seeding and how much of that grain he
[Mr. Castleden.l
wishes to deliver for the crop year to his own wheat pool, into Pacific, or into Federal Grain or the U.G.G. or whatever company it is.
On that basis, with the cars coming to that point, the local station agent can allocate them to the elevators proportionately. It might not be exact, but at any rate it would give the farmer the right to deliver his grain to the elevator of his own choice as nearly as it is humanly possible to do so. We had difficulty presenting this case in the standing committee on agriculture last year. We had difficulty making people understand that underneath this whole thing was a basic principle for which the farmer was fighting, and which he wanted established because he saw without it great danger to his own organization and his own rights.
The matter was brought before the committee at the meeting of the 20th of May, 1954, I believe. The question of congestion was explained, but it still did not prove to us why, if the wheat pools wanted to do 70 per cent of the business at a particular point, they should not get 70 per cent of the box cars and should be allowed only 40 per cent. The box cars were there. It is the farmer's own business, and surely he should not be compelled to take his business to the opposition. I think the people of Canada doing business would protest most vehemently if they were compelled to do business with other than their choice. At that time the Minister of Trade and Commerce said, as found at page 517 of the proceedings of the committee:
I think the problem in the farmers' minds is: how much grain can they market, not with any one particular agency, but how much grain can they market? That is the over-all problem.
That was a problem too. They can still deliver the same amount of grain through the same box cars. The pool elevator agent will get out the box cars just as quickly as the line elevator company if they are spotted in front of his elevator. The minister went on to say:
We are going to try to solve this problem of car distribution, but if we do not solve it no great principle is going to be violated. No one is going to have any serious loss.
There may be no serious loss in any one year. Perhaps it is only 4 or 5 cents a bushel, but bit by bit it adds up. The minister said no great principle was being violated. I should like to inform the house that we and the farmers feel a very serious and basic principle is being violated. The farmer sees a personal right being taken away. He sees the organization he has established being ruined. I should like the house to understand that the operations of the Winnipeg grain exchange probably represent private industry carrying on

business at its worst. If the people who support private enterprise want to know why the western farmers are against private enterprise, the best evidence they can find is the way private enterprise operators on the Winnipeg grain exchange have become millionaires over the years at the farmers' expense.
The only weapon the farmer has with which to fight is the co-operative organization built by himself. That is the means by which he has fought the battle throughout the years. When he sees his organization being destroyed by any means at all, but particularly when it seems to be in an underhanded way and he cannot get at the root of the trouble, then he feels very deeply about it. I have a letter here from a farmer in my constituency. He says that car distribution is terrible at that point, and goes on to say that the local agent has dropped from about 42 per cent last year to 28 per cent. In other words, he used to be getting 42 per cent of the grain at this point and it has dropped to 28 per cent. It used to be one of the best co-operative points in the whole district, but the agent is down to 28 per cent this year.
The rest of the wheat pool farmers in that district have been compelled to deliver what grain they have delivered to the private companies which have been their opposition. What disturbs them is the danger that this situation may become permanent. It is getting worse and worse. Each year the wheat pool reports a smaller and smaller percentage of the grain handled going through their elevators. More and more each year wheat pool farmers are compelled to deliver to the other elevators where there is space. The space is there because of the allocation of box cars. Wheat pool elevator points have found the situation particularly difficult, even in the areas where they are the only elevators at the particular points. They find that box cars are sent to other points and not to them.
The situation looks rather serious to the farmer and the wheat pool because they feel that through the allocation of the box cars their whole business is threatened permanently. They see what the Winnipeg grain exchange and the line companies would like to do. Their attack on the wheat pools is an effort to discredit the wheat pools and the wheat board. You can discredit the Canadian wheat board if you can get the farmers feeling that there is something wrong. You can discredit the wheat pools if the farmers think there is something wrong with the way cars are allocated.
We feel that a serious mistake was made in the past year in that through some machinations the Canadian wheat board 50433-230
Canada Grain Act
undertook to allocate orders to the various grain companies on a particular basis. We have had difficulty in finding out exactly how the board does operate, but I understand that when they sell a certain quantity of grain they allocate the grain orders to the various companies. If they allocate so many hundreds of thousands of bushels to the wheat pool they say, "You are to send us 400 cars of No. 4 wheat".
I understand that the wheat pool, as nearly as I can find out, is then supposed to say where it will get the No. 4 wheat and the different points to which the box cars should be sent. As a result the farmers in one area will say that they are in the wheat pool elevator at that point and cannot get any cars. Apparently the head office has sent the box cars somewhere else. I do not think any better method could be found to make the wheat pool committees and supporters angry at their own head office. If that is the system under which the matter is being handled, then I suggest it is time something was done about it.
Earlier this session I put certain questions on the order paper in an attempt to find out what was the basis under which cars were being allocated to the various companies. These are the three questions I asked:
1.	What is the basis for the allocation of grain shipping orders to the various elevator companies, as now used by the Canadian wheat board?
I just asked what the basis was.
2.	When was the present system of order allocation put into operation?
3.	How were the percentages for shipping orders as between elevator companies arrived at?
Has it been a 10-year basis? Have they taken any one particular year? Have they taken a free delivery year? The farmers would like to know the basis under which the wheat board is operating, because that will determine to a large extent the percentage of the business the wheat pool now is allowed to do. If they are only going to get 48 per cent of the shipping orders then they are only going to do 48 per cent of the business that year. If the wheat board decides under this system that they are only to get 42 per cent, then that is all the business they can possibly do even though 60 per cent of the farmers in the province of Saskatchewan may desire to do their business with the wheat pool.
That is where the danger lies. These are the replies I received:
1. It is not the policy of the Canadian wheat board to disclose details of its current operations nor the competitive position of various elevator companies in their capacity as agents of the board.
The answers to questions 2 and 3 were, "See answer to No. 1." I was not asking them

Canada Grain Act
to disclose their current operations. I wanted to try to find out by some means how shipping orders were at present being allocated, on what basis, and how the board determined which elevator company would be chosen. I say that because they can determine permanently whether an elevator company will grow or will be wiped out, through the allocation of these shipping orders and box cars. This is the kind of information we want.
The thing that makes farmers particularly suspicious about this is that in past years the box cars that went to various points were apparently taken there by the elevator company, and apparently the elevator company shipped them out to the particular districts under the orders of the transport controller. The man who was on loan as transport controller was a member of the board of grain commissioners. Now, that member of the board of grain commissioners was previously president of the Winnipeg grain exchange, and as transport controller he had wide powers. We cannot find out today who is responsible for this thing; we can only look at the result. The result has been that the line elevator companies have been increasing in power and the wheat pool cooperative organization has been decreasing in power.
The farmers see in this a threat to their organization built around the establishment of the old co-operative, the only weapon they have with which to fight for justice. It is for this reason we are introducing this bill now for the third time. Under the provisions of the bill the allocation of box cars at delivery points would be made according to the farmers' wishes. It is only a simple, basic right. Surely its administration is not too difficult. If cars were going to be delivered to a point they could be delivered at the elevators in proportion to the farmers' wishes. It does not help to hide the whole thing behind a screen of uncertainty, or to say no one knows whose responsibility it is. It does not help to give answers like this, that it is not our policy to disclose the operations of the board. I was not asking for disclosure of the operations of the board, but surely the allocation of box cars and the allocation of business is the business of the farmer.
The members of the farm co-operative organizations are aroused. For years they have accepted the excuse that the trouble was due to congestion and nothing could be done about it. They were told, "You want to sell grain, and we are doing what we can. We might not get all the cars out to each elevator." The farmers have taken that excuse for five or six years and each year the
IMr. Castleden.]
result has been exactly the same. They have ended up with less and less business and the opposition has had more and more business.
Today the wheat pool is making its protest. In the past year at their annual meeting the members of the wheat pool organization protested loudly and stated they felt there was an injustice to them; their patience was exhausted. They have heard excuses. They have heard people passing the buck and saying, "It is not my responsibility, it is his." Another says the responsibility belongs to the railways, and the railways say it is the transport controller. The transport controller says, "I have nothing to do with it."
I am going to say, Mr. Speaker, that in this fight the farmer is not going to give up easily. There is a basic right here that he feels is being violated. It is a right that should not be denied to any Canadian. It is part of his fight for existence. He has seen years of toil go into the production of wheat which he had to sell at less than half of what it cost him to produce. On the other hand, in the years before the wheat board he has seen the annual crop of millionaires coming out of the Winnipeg grain exchange and he is not going to see the wheat board wiped out. He is going to fight through his co-operative organization.
If this protest is not enough, he will make a more violent one. In this fight I can say this, that we are all very proud to be on the side of the farmer.

speechtext:
It is somewhat disadvantageous to have only one hour for the discussion of a matter of such great interest to the farmers of western Canada. The hon. member for Provencher took about 10 minutes of this hour, the hon. member for Acadia about 10 minutes and the hon. member for Yorkton between 20 and 25 minutes. Since hon. members on the government side of the house are always invited to express their opinion, it does not leave too many minutes in which we may do that. I can assure you that I shall try to do so in less time than it has taken the hon. member for Yorkton.
Much of the discussion has centred around the wishes of the farmers in western Canada. During the last several weeks many of us have received letters from farmers, not relating so much to this particular bill but merely expressing the opinion of those who wished to deliver to the elevator of their choice. I do not think there has ever been any government that has been more susceptible to the wishes of the western farmer than this government. Unfortunately what we are trying to decide, or at least what I am trying

to decide, is how many farmers in western Canada want this bill. Who are the farmers in western Canada who asked the mover of this bill to introduce it in this House of Commons? That is what I want to know, and that is what I am going to find out.
During the course of the last few weeks we have received a great number of letters. The letters are not all in agreement. I think they are mostly from pool members, and some of them are from pool delegates. Some of them are from farmers saying they want the right to deliver not only to the elevator of their choice but to more than one elevator. They happen to be living between two towns, and they want the right to change from one town and elevator to the other. It would seem to me, from the contents of the letters, that the farmers are somewhat fearful of being frozen to one elevator. Unless they choose one elevator and stay with that elevator for a crop year, then I see no advantage whatever in permitting an amendment to the Canada Grain Act that will allow a farmer to stipulate the elevator of his choice.
We want more unanimity of opinion on this matter. I do not know of one Liberal member who has received one letter from any grain grower in Alberta or Manitoba favouring this bill or suggesting that he be allowed to choose an elevator. Now, shall the government enact legislation to suit one area of this country, or shall the government take into consideration the wishes of the farmers of western Canada, or of all Canada for that matter? They are all affected. I would suggest to the farmers of western Canada that they get together and make a decision as to what they want. After they have made that decision they will not find any government that will be more sympathetic to their wishes.
We have heard about the wishes of the farmers of western Canada. We have heard that the farm organizations of western Canada are in favour of what is here proposed. I want to know what farm organization asked the hon. member for Assiniboia to introduce this bill into this House of Commons. Would he kindly stand up and answer? What farm organization in western Canada asked the hon. member for Assiniboia to introduce this measure into this House of Commons; that is what I want to know. I am waiting for an answer. If there is not an answer, then there is only one conclusion, and that is that the farmers of western Canada do not want it. Because if they did want it they would not ask an opposition member who has no responsibility, particularly a socialist member who has absolutely no influence in this House of Commons or 50433-2304
Canada Grain Act
anywhere else, to bring a measure of this kind before a responsible government.
If farm organizations did ask him to do that, then why do not those same farm organizations go out into Saskatchewan and ask the Liberal opposition members in the legislature to bring the Rand formula, or any other measure for that matter, before the socialist government in that province? If a Liberal member ever did that, then I say such legislation before the socialist government in Saskatchewan would last about as long as a snowball in hades.
I want the hon. member for Assiniboia to tell us what organization asked him to bring this measure before the House of Commons. And if he was not asked, why has he brought it here? I would ask him what political organization asked him to bring it here. Perhaps he will say it was the farmers' union. The situation that has been described here is one that would lead us to believe that the farmers in western Canada are very mad. Personally I would like to deliver to the elevator of my choice, because I was brought up with farm organizations. I was one of the original signers of the wheat pool agreement, and I have never missed an opportunity to support not only the wheat pools but other co-operative organizations.
If the farmers are mad now, then I would not like to face them two months after this legislation, if it were accepted, was brought into operation. I would not like to see their looks if there was a shortage of box cars, with one elevator full of grain and other elevators empty and the farmers without money. If they were not given the right to move around, then I would like to know how long this legislation would last in western Canada.
So I say the farmers would be a whole lot madder after the passage of legislation of this kind, if severe congestion conditions developed. Such conditions would not be the result of government policy, or government organization, but would be the result of natural conditions that could not be eliminated or helped by anyone. It might be that some would favour those conditions, because we have had some crop during these last years, for which most of us are grateful. But why attempt to compel the government to enact legislation to correct a situation that natural conditions brought about? After those natural conditions have passed I do not think anyone in western Canada would suggest that those same conditions would often be repeated. They have not, up to this time.
The wheat pool organizations have had as high as 53 per cent of the wheat in western

Canada Grain Act
Canada, and they are now reduced to about 43 per cent, or a 10 per cent reduction. The farm grain handling organizations in Manitoba and Alberta perhaps would do even better under the present distribution of box cars than they would by an allocation of box cars through designating the elevator of one's choice.
That is why we do not receive letters from pool members in Manitoba and Alberta. That is why we do not receive letters from pool low-point deliveries in Saskatchewan, where the pools have been receiving only 23 per cent of the grain during these past years. Those pool members would like to increase their deliveries at those points. What works in one place works differently in another. But the over-all picture is one of reduced handling by pool elevators.
If there is any member in the house or any member of any organization in western Canada-any grain handling firm, pool organization, farmers' union or anyone else -who is willing to take on the allocation of box cars in this country, let us have his name and we will give that name every consideration, and wish him good luck in his new position. Because immediately he will have to endeavour to satisfy everybody in western Canada. This does not mean that we are indisposed. All we are looking for is something that will work in the interests of all the people of western Canada. We have no guarantee that this will work; and until we do have, then I do not think any socialist or any other government would consider legislation that at least would not have some assurance of success, or that would have to be repealed within a very short time.
If the farmers of western Canada cannot agree on what they want in the matter of deliveries at grain handling points, then do not expect the government to force agreement upon them. The initiative must be left with the farmer. That is the place to apply it, with the farmers themselves. They should decide what they want. It should not be just one group of farmers or a certain number of farmers in any organization. It should be all the farmers, before any responsible government can cater to their needs. I repeat that no government is more willing to give consideration to the matter than this one.
So I say to the hon. member for Assiniboia that his bill does not come here with the authority it should have. I say to the hon. member for Assiniboia that he should withdraw the bill on his own authority, personally, if he has no authority from any farm organization.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just before five o'clock I had quoted from a speech by Dr. Hannam regarding the conference of the international federation of agricultural producers held at Nairobi. We in this group agree with the findings of that conference. We feel

that surpluses should not be eliminated by a reduction in production but rather by an expansion of markets through distribution of goods to needy people. At home we feel we can expand markets by increasing social services and welfare payments; and to the extent that expanding markets and private enterprise fail to provide jobs, national projects should be instituted by the federal government in conjunction with the provincial and municipal governments, thereby expanding the purchasing power of the people and still further sustaining demand.
Abroad, when foreign exchange and balance of payments difficulties occur, we should be prepared to accept sterling and in certain cases also currency of other foreign nations. In the United States of America, under the agricultural trade development assistance act, $1 billion is being made available for that purpose. Goods worth $1 billion can be sold for foreign currency. Unfortunately, in the United States they allowed the situation regarding these surpluses to get out of hand before instituting proposals of that kind.
Instead of continually criticizing the United States for making surplus goods available to foreign nations by means outside the ordinary channels of trade, we should do likewise in this country. We should give strong support to the proposals that have been made from time to time by the food and agriculture organization to set up a world food board, or agencies such as the international commodity clearing house. We believe the adoption of a two-price system would help to stabilize farm prices at a fair level; but the only real solution is to provide a total market. That would require a change in our financing so that a deficiency of purchasing power, resulting in a lack of effective demand, could be met by financing through the Bank of Canada.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the budget speech delivered to the house in April by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) opens the door to an innumerable variety of subjects for discussion. The press has had a great deal to say about the budget and comments have been largely favourable. It has even been likened to an election budget, or a convention budget, as the member for Broadview (Mr. Hees) said, among others.
Had the present government not enjoyed the confidence of the people for such a long time, and were not this confidence continuously increasing, I hardly think the budget would be such as to save an administration
The Budget-Mr. Legare in distress. It is a practical budget, based on present economic conditions and possibilities for the current year. The new minister, then, deserves the congratulations of the house and of the whole country for this, his first budget. A greater tax reduction would have been quite popular but anyone familiar with the present international situation and mindful of the threat of aggression will admit that, against its will, parliament has still to devote large amounts to national defence which could be used for a number of other purposes if peace were established.
I shall limit myself today to two topics only, immigration and the economic survey, announced in the budget speech.
The present government policy with respect to immigration causes me to wonder somewhat. Should we continue to admit some
150,000	immigrants a year to Canada until such time as the employment situation is. more stabilized?
Some economists believe that immigration* even intensive immigration, is the key not only to our expansion but to our economic progress. We are told that our natural resources are plentiful, that our production should be larger and that an increase in population would mean a greater number of consumers. So far so good, and the majority of the people will go along with that equation.
But what price that equation when we read in the newspapers that thousands of immigrants are out of work in western Canada, while hundreds of others are looking for work in the province of Quebec.
It seems that a large proportion of immigrants turn to seasonal jobs, such as farming in western Canada or mining or forestry in the province of Quebec. Consequently thousands of men, with a large proportion of immigrants, are thrown on the labour market during the off seasons.
On the other hand, we cannot contemplate offering permanent jobs to the immigrants while leaving the seasonal jobs for our present population.
Therefore, so long as our climate remains as changeable as it is today, our seasonal industries will keep on disturbing our labour market.
Quebec was once in a much more favourable position than it is today, especially when lumbering operations were conducted in wintertime. Our farmers or their sons, as soon as the crops were in, were then making for the forest to take up lumbering. Many

The Budget-Mr. Legare labourers from our urban centres also took advantage of the interruption of public works and house building during the winter to take up wood-cutting. Today, as I already mentioned previously in this house, the procedure is reversed, and lumbering operations often start in the summer, with the result that the number of unemployed is much larger in the winter. There are also the Ungava mines where operations are to be interrupted during the winter on account of the temperature which prevails during that season; thousands of workers, of whom many are immigrants, will become unemployed. And these are only a few examples. The problem, in my opinion, is more complicated than one would imagine and the co-operation of all the industrial leaders and the governments will be required in order to bring it to a solution.
I am in favour of immigration as long as the country benefits from it and its present population does not suffer from it. The immigrant himself, who has been attracted to Canada by the popularity of our country abroad, does not deserve to suffer the hardships of unemployment, particularly if he left a regular and permanent job in his own country.
When too much attention is given to the economic aspect of immigration, the human aspect is often forgotten. Our country needs consumers and is able to absorb millions of them, but these consumers represent an asset for us only as long as they produce and are not unemployed.
This problem which is one of the main causes of concern for the government should be placed on the agenda of the royal commission which is going to examine our economic position and its future. Our economy is linked to our productivity, which in its turn is dependent upon our population and foreign markets. Today, there are two seemingly weak links in the web of our economy: our production cannot find enough consumers and our consumers do not enjoy stable enough employment.
In my humble opinion, the proposed royal commission should more particularly try to find the causes of unemployment, study the effects of seasonal industry on the labour market and suggest the remedies which would help not only to give employment more stability, but to find work for a greater number of immigrants.
Until then, if the hon. Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickersgill) or the

hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) can bring evidence before the house to show that our immigration policy does not tend to increase the number of unemployed, I know they will render a great service to many hon. members in this house.
I have listened closely to the brilliant speech of the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Crestohl) in favour of immigration, and, despite his many quotations, he was unable to dispel my doubts.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, I am in favour of increasing the population of this country by all accepted and acceptable means, but only when it can be proved, otherwise than with theories, that the arrival of immigrants, far from increasing unemployment, is creating new jobs.
I am satisfied that the opinion I have just expressed is shared by a number of my fellow citizens. They do not know what to think of our immigration policy, and they are right.
To go in for selective immigration, to attract here foreign skilled labour which is not to be found in this country, that is fine. But that we should admit and attract from overseas unskilled workers, farmers who have never in their lifetime so much as touched a farm implement, jacks of all trades without a trade, as we now have them in this country by the thousands seeking employment, that is what many people cannot understand.
Oh, I know very well that the Progressive Conservatives in this house would like to see the government intensify immigration. We never take in enough immigrants, according to them. Instead of 150,000 we should admit 200,000, 300,000 and 400,000 annually. But who is it, in this house, who have been crying blue ruin because we have thousands of people out of work? Who, among them, could tell the house where the unemployed are capable of finding work at this time and where the thousands of immigrants who are about to disembark will find jobs?
Mr. Speaker, I will conclude by expressing the hope that soon the government will be in a position to show the house with figures to prove their contention that immigrants are not responsible for the present employment situation and that the present immigration policy is such that it is truly beneficial to this country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the subject under discussion is supposed to be the budget. I use that expression because

I think almost everything has been discussed in this debate as well as the budget. This budget does not seem to inspire any particular enthusiasm. I have heard it dissected by those who are opposed to the government; I have heard it praised by those on the government benches, and I still lack enthusiasm for it. It is not an inspired budget. It is a milk and toast budget. It is a wishy-washy budget. It does not get anyone very excited, least of all myself.
I was interested in hearing the comments of my own townspeople in regard to it, and I found the same apathy there I have noticed elsewhere. However, I should like to report one or two of the things some people talked to me about in regard to these financial measures. One was the injustice of the $60 ceiling on the contribution toward old age pensions under the income tax. In my opinion that is unjust, and most of the people with whom I talked agreed with me.
Another thing they talked to me about was the refusal of the government to make medical expenses deductible from the first dollar for purposes of income tax, as has been recommended at various times in measures introduced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). When we talked about the fact that there was a little easement in income tax the question immediately arose as to why the level of exemptions was not raised; why that method was not used rather than the other. To the man with the small income the actual dollar relief is small indeed.
Those are some of the things they talked to me about in connection with the budget. Then I had a visit from some of my friends who are automobile dealers and who indicated to me that they felt they had been treated with some injustice. While they welcomed the remission of 5 of the 15 per cent excise tax on automobiles, they resented the fact that they had some new cars on hand on which they had already paid the tax and there was no means by which they could get back that tax money unless this government was prepared to return it. They approached me as they have other hon. members. I have heard their plea put forward here by members of all political parties, including the government party, that something might be done in that regard.
As one might suspect from my treatment of the budget, I rise tonight to say a word or two about something else, namely the catastrophe that has just occurred in my own province and city. We had entered upon this year of 1955, this fiftieth anniversary, with pride and high hope, and it was a tremendous disappointment to us that we had to
The Budget-Mr. Knight suffer at the hands of the weather as we have done during this past week. I am referring to the storm which occurred in Saskatchewan.
My city was in the path of that particular storm, which did a great deal of damage. Hon. members no doubt have been reading the headlines in the papers. I have one here, but I would draw attention to the fact that these headlines refer not to the day after the storm but to the day before the storm, or to the day on which the storm occurred. The storm completed the devastation. The Saskatoon Star-Phoenix of Tuesday, May 3, indicates that there will be a drastic cut in wheat acreage amounting to an estimated one-third to one-half in some areas.
We are told that this was the wettest April on record. The normal precipitation is -5 inches, but this month we have had 3 [DOT] 38 inches. Anyone who has lived in Saskatchewan as long as I have, which is 45 years, will appreciate that this is a most unusual occurrence in the month of April. Generally all through the spring we look with anxious eyes at any cloud formation and hope we may get a good shower before June, or better still in June after the crop has been seeded. To start out in a welter of water such as there is this year is something so completely unusual that it has created a great deal of astonishment.
In a different column of this paper it is stated that cattle are being drowned in the Meadow Lake district in the overflowing streams, and that most roads in the province are impossible quagmires. These are some of the things that have happened to us this springtime, which we usually think of as being a warm and beneficent time of year. This year it has become something frightful and menacing.
As to the city of Saskatoon itself, there was an immediate disorganization of power, light, telephone and some transportation facilities. When the transportation broke down the mayor of the city declared a state of emergency. All three radio stations were off the air for some 15 or 20 hours. All this makes one think about what might happen in case of a war emergency. We all remember how the city of Montreal and some of the eastern cities were tied up by the great snowstorm of five or six weeks ago. This makes one realize what the danger would be if something more harmful than a snowstorm happened to one of these cities.
The city of North Battleford and some of the towns close to Saskatoon get their power and light from that city. When the power went off in those towns and cities they immediately tried to wire or phone Saskatoon

The Budget-Mr. Knight to find out what the trouble was, and ot course they discovered they could not get through. All means of communication-and when I say "all means" I mean it-had broken down. There was no way of getting any information as to what had happened. It was the next day before the people in those towns and cities knew what had happened to our city.
This storm is calamitous in more ways than one. If there had not been so much wind, as well as the snow, sleet and rain, we might have escaped comparatively free; but we had a combination of rain with sleet and snow. May I say that sleet, although it is common in this eastern part of the country, is very uncommon in the west. When the sun came out again people got around and tried to assess the damage. In the city communications began to be restored, traffic got under way again, and the temporary isolation was put to an end.
Here one should pay tribute to the people who handled that crisis; the city engineering departments and people who, I am told, worked for as long as 48 or 50 hours without a break, and the citizens who co-operated with these departments by lending their trucks and cars, the men of the Saskatchewan Power Corporation and of the Saskatchewan government telephone company, working unselfishly to establish communications.
How must one assess the damage from this particular storm? The provincial government was probably the public body which suffered most, because the provincial and municipal roads were washed out and in many cases impassable. The Saskatchewan Power Corporation, which supplies power and light to a great part of the province, and the telephone system were crippled. For miles the poles were down on the roads. The high voltage wires were down, which in itself formed a danger to the community. The damage to farms is incalculable and certainly, as yet, uncalculated, particularly in the eastern part of the province where there is water everywhere.
I have seen only one estimate of the damage, and that is by Professor Harrington, who is the head of the field husbandry branch of the University of Saskatchewan. His estimate was $50 million in terms of loss of the potential wheat crop. Notice that I said "wheat crop". We are well aware-in fact, it has been stated here today by one or two members who have spoken-of the important place wheat occupies in our national economy. On the basis of that loss alone one might claim that what has happened in our province might be termed a national disaster.

There are three ways, of course, in which this water will produce loss of wheat. The first is that land flooded in the low places will not be able to be seeded at all this year. Second, although they may dry up later, it will be too late to sow the flooded lands to wheat and they will have to be sown to coarse grains instead. Third, the late seeding of lands will produce a decreased yield and will make the crop a great deal more liable to an epidemic of rust, which hurt the province to such an extent this last year. The same thing, of course, applies to frost. There is no particular date when wheat should be seeded in the province of Saskatchewan, within a week or two, but Dr. Harrington estimates the date that wheat should be seeded is about May 7.

speechtext: How would you know when to seed wheat in Saskatchewan?

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would my hon. friend do me the courtesy to keep quiet? I have listened to his silly drivel often enough, and I have never interrupted him. I may say that I was growing wheat in this country when my hon. friend was coming across from North Dakota. Mr. Speaker, I beg your pardon for laughing, but my hon. friend always amuses me.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He should make you angry.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not want to get into an argument with the Minister of Agriculture. May I be allowed to continue. The sad part of this storm and the resulting damage is that a great many people who suffered last year are going to suffer again this year. I am thinking of the northeastern part of the province, Carrot River, Kamsack, and Nipawin districts where they suffered greatly last year and where this year the situation is going to be even more difficult. Perhaps this catastrophe will affect a greater number of people over a greater area than any of the Canadian catastrophes of late years.
If there is one good thing about catastrophes it is that they engender in people a spirit of help and co-operation. They bring people together. When a catastrophe happens, one remembers the pioneer days. When a person's barn was burned down or there was a prairie fire, or something of that kind, people came to help. In these catastrophes we may expect some assistance, and we are certainly expecting some assistance, from the dominion government.
I know it is not a popular philosophy, and in this house of practical men I almost hesitate to advance it, but perhaps we do at times emerge from hardships or struggle better and stronger for the suffering we have endured.

As 1 have said, that is not a popular philosophy and I do not expect my hon. friends to accept it. But we do need help, from our neighbours and friends. I believe that Saskatchewan, after this catastrophe, will once again prove its resilience. It is not the first time we have suffered catastrophes, whether of drought or of hail or of rust or of grasshoppers, and we have won through. In fact we have been able to contribute help to other parts of the country that have suffered the same sort of thing.
To come to the practical angle of this help for which we must ask the dominion government, we have been told in the last day or two that the premier of our province, Mr. Douglas, has been in touch with the Prime Minister in regard to this matter. Let me say that I thought the Prime Minister's attitude was reasonable when he stated that we must have an assessment from the provincial authorities as to what the damage actually is. Then we hope favourable consideration will be given by the dominion government, who might be reasonably expected to contribute a considerable amount in the way of help.
That is my plea and the reason I rise tonight. I have said something about the loss of provincial services, roads, light and power wires, and so on. Losses to individuals will of course be heavy. When I read about people, for instance, who have lost their cattle, I presume there will be property compensation for the loss of cattle, for buildings damaged by water, etc. But actually the great loss will be suffered by those to whom the making of a livelihood by the growing of grain will be denied for this year. We may as well face the fact that these people are going to be in dire straits by next winter, and the government may count on that in planning their assistance.
Someone has suggested an immediate start on a drainage program, and I think that is a good idea. So far as the land in the northeastern part of the province is concerned, I do know that the provincial government instituted a work and wages program in that region to compensate the people for the loss of their incomes last year. I hope that will be continued, but I suggest it will have to be continued on a much larger scale. I think the northeastern part of the province has some of the finest land in the world, certainly the finest land I have seen, but under present conditions it will have to be drained to be used at all.
That is one place where co-operation between governments might result in an immediate start which would have, as well
The Budget-Mr. Hellyer as its ultimate objective, the result of providing some work for people who for this year at least will not be able to make their usual living from their farms. Therefore my plea is that the government should co-operate immediately with the provincial government in starting some such program. That is the immediate necessity. In the long run the government should give generous consideration to whatever claims for assistance may be advanced by the province of Saskatchewan after some assessment of the damage has been made, and should render such assistance as may be judged reasonable in view of the experience with similar disasters in the past.

speechtext:
The additional purchasing power left in the hands of individual taxpayers will form the basis of increased demand for consumer goods and services. Inventories will be depleted and the tempo of our giant industrial machine will be accelerated.
The reduction in corporation tax will have a beneficial effect too, but only subject to the following conditions. If the increased profits are used for further industrial expansion it will provide jobs, while at the same time increasing our productive potential even further. If, on the other hand, the tax reductions are passed on to the consumers through lower prices for all products where there is an elastic demand, consumption and hence employment will increase.
Helpful as these improvements are, even coupled with the upswing in economic activity which appears to be taking place at the same time, it may still be necessary for something further to be done in order to provide jobs for those unemployed at the present time and those entering the labour force. There are many ways in which economic stimulus can be provided, but some of them are much more effective and more suitable than others. I should like to discuss one of these possibilities.

The Budget-Mr. Hellyer
I think the time has come when the federal government should embark on the construction of a system of federal roadways, and I should like to suggest that $2 billion should be earmarked for this purpose, to be spent over a five-year period. The reason I say a federal system of roadways is that I believe only in this way can a country of ten individual jurisdictions hope to have a consistently adequate arterial road system. It is true that a start has been made in the form of the joint enterprise known as the trans-Canada highway. It is because of the experience associated with this road that I propose that the federal system should be built, financed and maintained by the federal government. Some of the provincial governments have shown considerable ineptitude in getting proper value for money expended on highways, in particular where the money was raised by the federal government and handed over to them. I think we could expect good value if such a project were administered by this government, and there is no one better qualified to direct such a project than our own Minister of Public Works.
What are the implications of such a system? They are material to a number of individual problems, and it is necessary to examine several of them. First let us consider commerce. There is no need of reciting all the developments which inevitably follow new transportation routes. I do not think anyone will deny that along such a system of roads would spring up new towns and cities, new factories and facilities, new enterprises and developments of all kinds. The stimulus to our commerce generally would be so substantial that it is difficult to project. It can be safely stated, however, that it would be sufficient to warrant the expense and in the long run would repay the cost many times over.
A direct and immediate function of such a system of arterial roads would be a tremendous improvement in our civil preparedness. There are those who state that in this day of atom and hydrogen bombs civil defence is merely a myth. I cannot and will not subscribe to such a theory of hopelessness. There is an excellent possibility that we would obtain three or four hours' notice of attack by any prospective enemy. With even such a short notice, provided the necessary highways for egress from our cities had been built and our civil defence organizations had been properly trained, we could hope to evacuate a large proportion of the inhabitants from any or all of our major cities.
Under today's conditions any plan would be very difficult to implement. An attempt to evacuate the city of Toronto at the present

time would cause one of the most fantastic traffic jams in history, and it would take hours to untangle it and get the people either out of or back into the city. To be effective and even moderately adequate we would need three or four eight-lane limited access highways leading out of the city in various directions. This would involve a number of arterial collector roads running through the city itself, such as an extension southward of the present highway 401, an eight-lane Don valley expressway from the waterfront right north to the city limits and beyond, the Spadina road extension, and a widening of the Toronto by-pass highway to a minimum of eight lanes.
It is interesting to note that the usual lack of foresight has been shown in respect to this last-mentioned road, which is only four lanes and will be inadequate 48 hours after it has been opened from the Queen Elizabeth highway to the Kingston road. The eight-lane provision would have to extend outward from our major cities at least 200 miles, because otherwise the congestion at the end of the wide road would work backward and destroy its usefulness. By having several such roads leading from each city it would be possible to use all of them, with the exception of the one over which severe radioactive fall-out would be expected, having due regard to the direction of the wind at the time of any imminent attack.
These facilities for egress should be provided for all our major cities, and proportionate facilities for any others which could reasonably be expected to become even secondary targets. This would certainly include Halifax, Montreal, Ottawa, Toronto, Hamilton, Windsor, Winnipeg, Edmonton, Calgary, Vancouver, etc. Should an attack come and as a result of our lack of foresight the necessary escape routes not be available, it would be a dreadful thing to feel responsibility for such a grievous error.
A third important aspect of a continentwide highway system would be our tourist trade. It was most disturbing to me to note that in the year 1954 we had an adverse balance with the United States in respect to tourist business. Something must be done to reverse this situation. An examination of the complaints of United States tourists shows that only two are significant, our roads and our accommodation. We have so many wonderful attractions which our United States friends are anxious to enjoy that it seems a shame we are our own worst enemies in making it so difficult for this great luxury loving tourist inflow.
The first half of the problem would be overcome by a really adequate system of

transcontinental and defence arterial highways. The system would, of course, have to be joined to the United States system at all important border crossing points such as St. Stephen, New Brunswick; Rouses Point and Stanhope, Quebec; Cornwall, Niagara Falls, Fort Erie and Windsor, Ontario; Emerson, Manitoba; Estevan, Saskatchewan; Coutts, Alberta; and Pacific Highway port in British Columbia. There may be others, new places, which would also be worth while connecting up. It should also, of course, be connected with subsidiary highways into our various playground areas.
The other half of the tourist problem is, of course, to encourage the building along and throughout the system of great new accommodation centres such as our United States friends patronize and enjoy. These centres should be complete with facilities for sleeping, eating, automobile servicing and, where possible, recreation. Naturally such new and modern centres would be appreciated not only by our visitors but by our own citizens as well. Their building and maintenance would provide a great number of new job opportunities. We could, at the same time, further develop the art of service which is so apparent in some countries which specialize in the tourist business. We should also specialize in Canadian foods and fly the Canadian flag as our United States friends come here to enjoy something different and not just to witness an endless repetition of facilities similar to their own.
It is a fair question to ask how we could finance such a system of roadways. I propose that they should be paid for not out of current revenues but rather by having the cost amortized over a period of 20 or 25 years. The mechanics of this method of financing would have a tremendously stimulating effect on our economic set-up and the results, direct and indirect, would be most gratifying.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I think it is reasonable to affirm that any project which would have such a beneficial effect on our commerce, provide the foundation of civil defence and safety for millions of our citizens, and in many parts of our country increase our tourist trade three or fourfold, while at the same time providing directly and indirectly tens of thousands of new jobs for our people, is so important and so urgent that it should be proceeded with as quickly as properly engineered plans can be prepared.
