speechtext:
I propose discussing tonight, Mr. Speaker, the subject of dominion-provincial conferences. This subject is closely related to the Minister of Finance's budget speech,
The Budget-Mr. Churchill because he devoted several paragraphs to federal-provincial relations. I know that the word "dominion" has become a rather naughty word but it is not yet an unparliamentary expression, so perhaps I shall be able to use it during the course of my remarks. As I have consulted the reports of earlier conferences, I have found that until very recent years they were called dominion-provincial conferences. I find it so much easier to use that term.
I want to talk about what I call Canada's other parliament, that is the dominion-provincial conference which assembled in Ottawa just two or three weeks ago and which will reassemble in October. Canada's other parliament is composed of the Prime Minister and the 10 provincial premiers, assisted by their respective cabinet ministers. At the meeting on April 26 there were in attendance approximately 80 persons, representing all the provinces and the dominion government.
You will recall that meetings were held in the railway committee room. The first meeting was open to the public, with the result that there were more members of the House of Commons sitting in as observers than there were in this chamber. In fact for the two days of the conference the House of Commons could very well have been adjourned. The Prime Minister, and I presume the senior cabinet ministers, were either in constant attendance or very close at hand. I believe we were not able to continue the budget debate on Tuesday because the Minister of Finance wanted to be present at that conference. The press gallery had no other interest except the conference, and the public at large was awaiting with eagerness the reports of the conference because it was recognized that on it hinged much of great importance to Canada as a whole.
The Prime Minister recognized the great interest that was taken in the conference and, thanks to his kindness, I have in my hand a copy of the proceedings at the preliminary meeting. It is the unrevised edition, and the only words I propose to quote from it will be the words of the Prime Minister himself. Since he is present this evening, if there is anything wrong with the quotation he can make a correction. I notice on page 4 that he said:
Though this is only a preliminary meeting for the 1955 conference, it seems to have attracted a large amount of attention outside as well as inside this chamber.
I certainly agree with that; it attracted a great deal of attention. I propose to examine for a few minutes the history and purpose of dominion-provincial conferences. I will suggest that serious thought must be given to

The Budget-Mr. Churchill their development and to the long-term effect on the prestige, authority and development of the parliament of Canada, with particular reference to the House of Commons.
My attention was directed to this subject for two reasons, the first of which I have given; that was the intense interest in the conference which assembled here at a time when the House of Commons was in session. The second reason was that at that conference the Prime Minister took the opportunity of making a considered statement with regard to unemployment and set out certain proposals of the government.
Consider the circumstances. Parliament was in session, and had been sitting since early in January. The subject of unemployment had been under debate for a very considerable time on an amendment proposed by Her Majesty's loyal opposition. Eight days of debate had been devoted to that subject and many members on both sides of the house had spoken. Time after time the Prime Minister was asked to make a statement, to disclose government policy, but remained silent. Yet on the opening day of the dominion-provincial conference, in his opening address to the assembled delegates the Prime Minister dealt at some length with the subject of unemployment and presented the government's plan to deal with the emergency.
This to my mind, or in my experience, was one of the most outstanding instances of bypassing parliament. Frequently members of the opposition complain when cabinet ministers make statements of government policy at public meetings, or by means of press releases, when the House of Commons is in session. We think they should inform the House of Commons first. On this occasion the Prime Minister declared his policy first to the dominion-provincial conference.
The question arising, then, is this. Is the dominion-provincial conference a superior governing body in this dominion? Before that question can be answered one should look at the history of dominion-provincial conferences. That is exactly what I have done, and I shall pass on to the house the information I have gained. The subject, of course, is large and all-embracing, and the time at my disposal this evening is limited. I do not propose now to deal with all the aspects of dominion-provincial relations or go into detail to any great extent on some of these conferences; but here is the history I have found.
There were no conferences of this nature during the first 20 years after confederation. Then in 1887 the premier of Quebec invited

the premiers of the other provinces to attend an interprovincial conference in the city of Quebec. Ontario, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Manitoba accepted the invitation. Eight days were spent in deliberations among the premiers who were there, and the subjects they discussed were annual subsidies paid by the dominion to the provinces -which they wanted to have increased-and amendments to the British North America Act.
Fifteen years later, in 1902, at the same place, another interprovincial conference was held. Five premiers and nine cabinet ministers from the provinces were present, and the same topics were discussed.
In 1906 the then prime minister, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, was persuaded to assemble a conference at which the premiers of all nine provinces were present, along with their advisers. The conference, however, was mainly provincial. There were sessions at which members of the dominion cabinet sat in with the provincial premiers. The subjects discussed were subsidies, and a resolution was passed urging that the conference assemble annually.
Then in 1910 and 1913 two further interprovincial conferences were held, at which no representatives of the dominion cabinet were present. Similar subjects were discussed, plus representation in the House of Commons which, at that time, affected Nova Scotia particularly.
Then in 1918 Sir Robert Borden called a dominion-provincial conference. He and nine of his cabinet ministers were present. For the first time the chairman at one of these conferences was a dominion cabinet minister, the then minister of public works, Mr. Carvell. The conference was assembled just one week after the armistice, and the subject of postwar development of Canada was naturally of some importance. The main subjects which came up at that conference were soldier settlement, general land settlement, and the return of the natural resources to the prairie provinces. As nine cabinet ministers were present the opportunity was taken, during the course of the four-day conference, to discuss such matters as demobilization, reconstruction, employment, civil re-establishment, taxation, housing, technical education and highways. At the conclusion of the conference Sir Robert Borden thought it was rather useful, and suggested that similar conferences might be held at 10-year intervals.
In 1926 a three-day conference was held, attended only by the premiers of the provinces and their cabinet ministers. There was no representation from the dominion. Again they discussed subsidies and taxation.

The year 1927, Mr. Speaker, was the turning point or the watershed in so far as dominion-provincial conferences are concerned. The seven preceding conferences I have mentioned, with the exception of the one in 1918, had been interprovincial, and in the matter of agenda and subject matter had been largely under the control of the provincial premiers; and attendance, except for a few dominion cabinet ministers at three sessions in 1906, had been limited to provincial representatives. The year 1918 was the exception.
Since 1927 there have been seven dominion-provincial conferences, if I may count the two in 1950 as one. They have been called together on the initiative of the dominion government, and the conferences have acquired an importance in national affairs greatly exceeding their importance prior to 1927.
It was at the 1927 conference that the dominion government exercised its full weight and influence. Of the 46 persons present at the conference of cabinet rank, and I include premiers in that term, 18 were from the dominion. Similarly, in the conferences of 1935 and 1945 the dominion cabinet as a whole participated. These three conferences, those of 1927, 1935 and 1945, set the pattern of procedure and organization of dominion-provincial conferences. I am omitting reference to the conference of 1934, which was very briefly reported; I could find very little about it. I am omitting reference to the conference of 1941, which lasted two days, and I am omitting reference to the two conferences of 1950, one of which assembled in January to discuss constitutional matters, and the other in December to discuss fiscal arrangements.
These three conferences, of 1927, 1935 and 1945, have established a pattern for dominion-provincial conferences which is well worth examining. For example, in 1927 seven days were taken up in a discussion of a total of 40 subjects. These were grouped under three main headings, constitutional, financial, social and economic. Some of the subheadings selected at random are as follows: Senate reform, regulation of aircraft and flying operations, federal subsidies, taxation, customs and excise duties, agriculture, health, immigration, old age pensions, fisheries and Canadian nationality. In one form or other, all these subjects are under discussion almost every year in the House of Commons.
In 1935 the conference lasted five days. Six committees were set up to consider separately the following subjects: tourist traffic, mining development, agriculture and marketing, constitutional questions, unemployment and relief and financial questions. All of these
The Budget-Mr. Churchill again are subjects familiar to the House of Commons. The purpose of the committee discussions and reports of 1935 may be discovered in the words of Mr. Dunning, who was then minister of finance. He said, and I quote from page 37 of the 1935 report:
We are receiving these reports in order that they may be submitted to the appropriate legislative and administrative authorities as a foundation upon which these authorities can base effective policy.
In other words the conference was designed to provide a guide for the development of legislative programs. At the same conference the then prime minister, Mr. King, looked forward to establishing the dominion-provincial conferences on a permanent basis and this is what he said at page 9 of the same report:
This arrangement of continuity and permanence is necessary because co-operation between the dominion and the provinces is too vital a matter to be left entirely for intermittent conferences, and to correspondence between governments. Our secretarial arrangements and our proposed organization are based upon this desire to have permanence and continuity.
At the conference of 1945 dominion-provincial relations burst into full bloom. It was the twelfth in the series, the largest in attendance, the lengthiest and most impressive in subject matter. Sixty-eight persons of cabinet rank were present, assisted by 140 advisers and officials. Their printed proceedings cover 624 pages. They sat here in the House of Commons part of the time and in the Senate chamber on other occasions. The general topic of that conference was reconstruction, and the dominion proposals were put forward under these headings: financial arrangements, public investment, health, old age pensions, unemployment assistance and tax rental agreements. Once again I point out that these are subjects frequently mentioned in debates in the House of Commons.
The year 1955 has seen the commencement of another dominion-provincial conference which after a two-day session in April to draft and set the subjects for discussion in the fall, is due to reassemble in October. The subjects suggested by the various premiers as proper for the conference to consider cover almost the whole field of House of Commons activities. I have listed them all here, but I have not counted them, they are so numerous. However, there were notable exceptions; for example, external affairs, defence. The conference apparently decided to deal with unemployment, fiscal arrangements or taxation, resources development, health and welfare, and most likely will give consideration to holding more frequent conferences. Ever since 1887 the provincial premiers have been suggesting this, and a permanent secretariat.

The Budget-Mr. Churchill
Well, Mr. Speaker, I suggest this survey raises this question. Why are these dominion-provincial conferences necessary? The answer briefly seems to be that there is something wrong in the confederation that is Canada. These conferences seem very similar to international gatherings such as the United Nations, NATO, or commonwealth conferences. Heads of governments or cabinet ministers representing sovereign states meet together to solve pressing problems. Many of these international gatherings end in frustration. Some people have suggested that a federal union would be better for some of these purposes, for example, among the nations comprising the Atlantic community or among the nations of Europe.
Here in Canada we are reversing the process. We already have a federal union with elected representatives from all the provinces. Why then must the heads of the 11 governments of Canada meet in conference to make plans for the country as a whole? Not content with 11 governments for a population of 15 million, we are now engaged in an attempt to establish a twelfth government superior in functions and importance to the other 11.
The root of the problem seems to be in the field of taxation and administration. And, as I have noted, in all the conferences since 1887 the problem of fiscal arrangements, taxation or subsidies, has come to the fore. In 1945 the present Leader of the Opposition, (Mr. Drew) who was then premier of Ontario, summed it up as follows, and I quote from page 11 of the report of that year:
There is one fundamental weakness in the British North America Act which lies at the root of many of our difficulties. While the legislative powers of the dominion and provincial governments were defined with reasonable clarity, the division of taxing powers was left in a much less satisfactory position. The provinces were empowered to levy taxes in the field of direct taxation . . . whereas the dominion government was authorized to raise money by any form of taxation. We therefore have the anomaly that, while the powers of the provincial governments have been extended by judicial interpretation of their statutory powers, the dominion government has found it necessary over the years to occupy more and more the only field of taxation which was made available to the provincial governments.
The recurring theme throughout all these conferences from 1887 to the present day has been that these provincial responsibilities have been increasing while the financial resources have not been adequate, hence the conferences, hence the suggestions for more frequent meetings and for a permanent secretariat, hence also the growing importance of the conferences and their overshadowing of parliament.


The problem is clear; the solution has not yet been found. For the last 70 years provincial premiers and prime ministers have been attempting to solve this problem without success. It may yet be done through the medium of a dominion-provincial conference, but in the process we may witness, if these conferences are to continue at short intervals for another 70 years, the decline of the prestige, influence and power of the House of Commons.
The reason I say this, Mr. Speaker, is that the conferences, ever since 1927, are tending to range over the whole field of public interest and endeavour. What purpose is there in debating the subject of unemployment in the House of Commons if the policy in that regard is to be announced first to a dominion-provincial conference and the decision thereon to be dependent, perhaps, on the deliberations of that body? What purpose to debate the development of our resources if that is a subject for the conference in October? Why bother in the House of Commons with the subject of health and welfare if the conference has that on its agenda?
I do not suggest that provincial comments are not necessary and desirable on these and many other matters, but is a full-dress conference the best way to get provincial approval or disapproval? I notice that in his introductory remarks at the conference in April the Prime Minister mentioned that there were other means. He is reported at page 3 of the proceedings as follows:
Taking place between these main conferences, there have been many meetings of provincial and federal representatives on other and more specialized subjects. I think we may say that there is now more continuing and frequent contact between our government and their officers than ever took place before.
In my judgment there is ample opportunity for the dominion government to get the information it desires. Consider our position here under the federal union. The Canadian federal system is designed to give protection to the provinces through a fixed quota of members in the Senate, and to provide membership in the House of Commons through representation by population. The cabinet by custom and tradition recognizes the provinces in the distribution of portfolios. I doubt if the House of Commons has at any time since confederation been without a number of former premiers and former provincial cabinet ministers in its membership. In the two houses of parliament, if all vacancies are filled, there are 367 persons, each of whom has some knowledge of the problems of the province from which he comes. In every area of Canada there are officials of

the dominion government. Between the provincial capitals and Ottawa passes an endless stream of correspondence. The telegraph, telephone and aeroplane have made communication reliable, speedy and convenient.
It would be interesting to determine the results that have come from the twelve conferences which preceded the one called for this year. What new ideas, what new policies have been advanced following these conferences? Has anything happened at them that could not have been accomplished in the House of Commons? It would be interesting also to know the cost to the taxpayer of these conferences.
I am not unaware of the fact that the desire for dominion-provincial conferences originated with the provinces, nor that suggestions for such conferences have been put forward frequently in the House of Commons. Until April 26 I had not considered the implication of these conferences and their probable effect on parliament. I now entertain grave doubts as to their purpose and value if they follow the course of the conferences of 1927, 1935 and 1945, and if they become a permanent feature of our system of government; certainly so if we are to become dependent on them for the forming of policies for this dominion.
The purpose of these conferences, in so far as I can judge from reading the proceedings, particularly those since 1927, has been to set forth matters of policy, to prepare for legislative programs either dominion or provincial; and in this connection I referred to the remarks of Mr. Dunning at an earlier conference. I suggest that the proposals put forward at many of these conferences involved taxation, and taxation is a problem which concerns this House of Commons. Parliament should decide the amount of taxes to be levied on our people, not a dominion-provincial conference which has quite often indirectly set figures and quotas which resulted in taxation.
I am suggesting that by dealing with dominion-provincial conferences the executive here, the cabinet, is not fulfilling its responsibilities to the House of Commons itself. This is a place where government programs should first be put forward, not at conferences.

Certainly the problem of unemployment had to be dealt with, and dealt with quickly, but these suggestions could have been put forward here in the House of Commons. I am directing attention to the general problem of dominion-provincial conferences and their effect upon the House of Commons. An interruption with regard to a detail like that in my opinion is not in keeping with the thoughts which I am attempting to put forward.
I am putting these matters forward seriously, and with the hope that people will examine these suggestions I am making and perhaps be able to destroy them by their arguments. On the other hand, historians may discover later that in 1927, 1935 or 1945 occurred the beginning of the decline of the influence of the House of Commons, which we have heard mentioned on many occasions in the last few years.
However, I am coming rapidly to a conclusion. Throughout the course of these latest conferences mention was made that what was being held was just a conference, that there was nothing partisan about the discussion, that the parties were there to co-operate for the good of Canada as a whole. If they were just conferences, if there was nothing of a party nature about them, why have they been restricted just to government representatives?
I think sometimes we forget that our parliamentary system is dependent upon two forces interacting on each other. There is the government side, and there is the official opposition. I would suggest that conferences of this nature should be attended not only by the heads of the 11 governments of Canada but by the leaders of the official oppositions in the legislative assemblies of this country, along with their advisers.
If you carry this idea of dominion-provincial conferences to a logical conclusion, what happens? You have a government set up over and above the ones we now have, and the result would be a sort of small united nations assembly of Canada. What disturbs me is the effect of all this on the House of Commons.
I will conclude with this statement. Dominion-provincial conferences may continue to be a necessity for Canada. If so,

The Budget-Mr. Boucher they should be restricted to the core of the problem, the division of administrative responsibility between the dominion and the provinces, and the division of fields of taxation. Unless complete breakdown of the federal system is threatened, such conferences need not be held except at intervals of many years for any necessary review that may be required due to changing conditions. Dominion-provincial conferences established on a permanent basis holding more frequent meetings, conducted after the fashion of the conferences of 1927, 1935 and 1945, will develop into another parliament for Canada, and will result in the decline of the influence of the present House of Commons.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to participate in this budget debate I would like to congratulate the Minister of Finance on the presentation of his first budget. This budget was proposed to give us income tax reductions ranging from 2-8 per cent to 13-3 per cent, and gives at least 80 per cent of Canadians reductions ranging from 12-6 to 13 per cent, effective July 1 of this year.
I believe the Minister of Finance realized that business also needed a shot in the arm and consequently reduced corporation taxes, which will encourage manufacturers to expand plants and production, thus offering more jobs to Canadians. Corporations and businesses are like individuals in some respects. If the incentive is taken away because of exorbitant taxation and the shareholders are not getting a fair return on their investment, financial support is withdrawn, followed by loss of sales and loss of production which leads to lay-offs and unemployment.
This is a time to loosen up and encourage business to expand. The tax cuts are needed in Canada at the present time. We have a marvellous country, a marvellous future, and an almost incredible potential wealth. Our foundations are sound. But the government does not create one single item of tangible wealth. It does not grow any of our wheat, nor does it produce any of our steel, nor does it make any of the thousands of items that create what we now call our material standard of living. The government redistributes the people's wealth. It chooses where the taxes will come from and where the proceeds will go. The hon. member for Eglinton said the other day, and I quote, "This is a budget without any pattern. This is a budget that is not founded upon any principle".
Mr. Speaker, a shot of tonic was needed in our economy. We have had balanced budgets for 10 years or so, which is commendable.
fMr. Churchill.1
But this does not necessarily mean that we always have to have a balanced budget. The hon. members of the opposition in past years have been asking repeatedly for a reduction in income tax. Now, when the time is ripe for such a reduction, they claim it is a rosy budget and that the government is putting too much faith in the ability of the Canadian nation to develop our immense resources.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As far as I am concerned I am satisfied that the majority of the people living in the constituency I have the honour of representing in this house approve of this budget. Mr. Speaker, the constituency of Chateauguay-Huntingdon-Laprairie is a typical Canadian constituency where English and French-speaking Canadians live together in peace and harmony. Even if industries are a big factor in the economy of our constituency, agriculture remains its most important one, and the dairy industry its backbone. Forty per cent of the population of Chateau-guay and Huntingdon depend directly upon the dairy industry, and a much larger proportion of their population derive their income from it indirectly.
Those farmers are industrious, diligent and are attached to their work. Whenever one travels through their well-kept farms one has the impression that those farmers are prosperous. But we must not forget that last year's crop was very poor, almost to the point of failure. In many cases it will be necessary for my people to buy feed for their cattle and seed to sow this year's crop. For that very reason I wish to thank the Minister of Agriculture for taking positive action in the maintenance of the price of butter at 58 cents a pound. I know my constituents will appreciate this very much.
(Translation):
Because our farmers are progressive, because they are always anxious to add to their farm equipment as a means of increasing crop yields, they sometimes have to borrow. Our government, through the Canadian farm loan board, is trying to help farmers by making it easier for them to secure loans. Loans are granted up to a maximum of $10,000, which seems quite reasonable. The various systems of refunding those loans also seem quite favourable. Still, I wonder whether there is not room for improvement in certain particulars pertaining to the qualifications required for securing such loans.
For example, the Canadian farm loan board will not lend to farmers who hold parttime jobs elsewhere. But, is it not a fact that

most farmers who apply to the Canadian farm loan board are precisely those who wish to improve the yield of their lands, so as to make farming their full-time work. Is it not true too that those farmers who take part-time work in this way do so to earn extra cash because, as a result of inadequate equipment, they do not make enough out of farming to live on.
Those farmers have no other purpose than to practise farming exclusively, but not unless and until their lands can support them and their family adequately.
I am therefore of the opinion, Mr. Speaker, that these loans should be placed at the disposal of the farmers, even if they have to do part-time work outside the farm. It seems to me too that the farm loan board is far too strict on the score of mortgage guarantees required of applicants. As a notary practising in an agricultural district where lands are highly productive, I have had several opportunities of noticing how stringent were the board's requirements in this connection.
To my knowledge, a number of farmers have tried in vain to get loans from the Canadian farm loan board. After being turned down, they managed to borrow money from private sources, retired people with private means or from businessmen who would certainly have refused the loan if they had thought for a moment that the property to be mortgaged was of insufficient value to cover the amount of the loan.
I hope those remarks will receive favourable consideration so that in future our farmers will be able to obtain such loans without mortgage guarantees in excess of those asked for by private lenders.
A moment ago I was saying that the Chateauguay-Huntingdon-Laprairie riding derives its prosperity from the excellence of the work done by our farmers and the diversity of the industries established within its limits.
Therefore, I cannot defer to the arguments put forward by members of the various opposition groups who would have us believe that Canada is in the midst of a depression.
At times we may be faced, as in a few parishes in my county, with seasonal and temporary unemployment. However, I have no doubt that its present policy will enable the government to solve this problem once and for all. Already, in our region, we see a strong economic upswing.
The Budget-Mr. Boucher
I had the opportunity just recently of visiting a large textile mill in the Huntingdon district. I was pleased indeed to note a feverish activity in that mill. I take this opportunity to ask the government to consider seriously the problems facing that industry.
The leaders of the textile industry in my constituency are animated with the spirit of the pioneers of this country. They took chances with their money and placed at the disposal of their fellow citizens their great experience, so that today in Huntingdon we have mills providing employment to a great proportion of the population. The leaders of the textile industry were criticized for insufficiently modernizing their equipment. That criticism could not be levelled at the owners of the textile industries in my riding, because their equipment compares favourably with that of other manufacturers in this country and abroad. Labour is also excellent. Obviously, and it is all to the credit of the present government, our standard of living is equalled or surpassed only by the standard of living in the United States.
It will be readily admitted that it is not up to the government to come to the rescue of the lords of the textile industry who have failed to run their business efficiently. The others should, however, not suffer from unfair competition by nations less privileged in their standard of living. I submit these few remarks on the textile industry, because I am certain that the government will give them serious consideration.
The name of the other part of my riding, the Laprairie district, is now in everybody's mouth. This county, which, historically speaking, goes back to the seventeenth century, has always enjoyed great prosperity. The completion of the St. Lawrence seaway opens up the prospect of gigantic industrial development and, consequently, a much greater prosperity. Many industries are already paying fabulous prices for property adjacent the St. Lawrence river. Home building is growing apace and creating many jobs. Yet, these changes cannot but raise many problems, and I seize this opportunity to commend the government for having appointed as chairman of the St. Lawrence seaway project a man of such experience and such capacity for work as the Hon. Lionel Chevrier, who has proved his mettle for many years in and outside this house. The appointment of the hon. Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) should also be men-

The Budget-Mr. Boucher tioned. His vast knowledge and his long parliamentary experience in the Quebec legislature had marked him for such a post. No doubt that under their leadership all the problems relating to the St. Lawrence seaway project will be solved.
Among those problems there is the price that should be granted to the land owners to be expropriated. Located in one of the most enchanting districts, across from the Lachine rapids and near the metropolis of Canada, these properties have an exceptional market value. And here, Mr. Speaker, allow me to make a special reference to the farms which are being expropriated. Apart from having an excellent market value, due to their privileged location, for housing projects, these farms are also considered to be among the best for market-gardening. Deals concerning market-gardening farms located in the same area are abundant proof of my statement, since the average price arrived at in these deals was about $1,500 per acre, without any buildings. I have no doubt that the St. Lawrence seaway authority will take these facts into consideration and adequately compensate the people who are being expropriated.
Before resuming my seat, I wish also to draw the attention of the seaway authorities to the fact that the very great majority of those expropriated will not yet have been paid when the time comes for them to leave their homes, about the first of June next, if my information is correct. I am told that in the past, in similar circumstances, the government has agreed to pay at once an amount representing 80 per cent of his offer when the parties had failed to come to an understanding. It would be unfair, I feel, to tell those people of whom a sacrifice is being asked in the general interest of the community, those people who did not wish to move elsewhere and change their way of living, who have worked on those farms for many generations since the time when our country was but a colony: "Go away, that is the law; whether you have money or not, you must move elsewhere; it is not our problem, it is up to you to agree to a settlement". Such a stand is not that of a Liberal government; I am convinced that the seaway authorities will understand their duty and thus maintain the confidence that the citizens of Chateauguay-Huntingdon-Laprairie have had for such a long time in the Liberal party.

When the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne was taking place in 1944 the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) spoke. And may I say, when we are discussing the speech from the throne, that the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Studer) is entirely wrong when he makes reference to items which he says are included in that speech; because when the address is given we find quite clearly, as is indicated in this year's speech from the throne, that the hon. member moving the address in reply said, as reported in the translation of his remarks at page 11 of Hansard:
That the following address he presented to His Excellency the Governor General of Canada.
To His Excellency the Right Honourable Vincent Massey, C.H., Governor General and Commander in chief of Canada:
May it please Your Excellency:-
And this was what we were voting on.
We, Her Majesty's most dutiful and loyal subjects, the House of Commons of Canada, in parliament assembled, beg leave to offer our humble thanks-
And so on. We were not voting on any particular item in the speech from the throne. We were simply offering our thanks to the Governor General for having addressed us. It may be that the hon. member does not know this. However, we will come to that a little later on.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
When the hon. member voted to defeat the government, would there have been family allowances if his vote had defeated the government?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order. The hon. member for Bow River may continue.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: When we did vote on that we were voting confidence or non-confidence in the government. I have never, in the 20 years I have been here, voted confidence in this government, and I do not intend to start now.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is why you voted against family allowances.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He did not.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The speech from the throne in 1944 said this, in part:
The family and the home are the foundation of national life. To aid in ensuring a minimum of well-being to the children of the nation and to help gain for them a closer approach to equality of opportunity in the battle of life, you will be asked to approve a measure making provision for family allowances.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And you voted against it.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Governor General himself has said there was no measure in his speech dealing with family allowances, but that "you will be asked". The hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek does not know his grammar sufficiently well to recognize the future tense. But this clearly says, "You will be asked to approve a measure", and of course that statement was true. Again the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek cannot understand English when he sees it.
Now, when we come to speaking on the address in reply, if the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek had taken the trouble to read the record he would have got it straight. The hon. member for Acadia, speaking at that time, said this as reported at page 153 of Hansard for February 3, 1944:
I very much welcome the government's proposal to pay family allowances. This is a step in the direction we have been advocating for a number of years. We first began to advocate something of this kind in this house in 1936; and I think most hon. members will recall how the suggestion that money should be paid directly to individuals outside the industrial system was scoffed at in this house. We were continually told that we were advocating something for nothing. However, apparently the government now see the light and are proposing to issue money directly to consumers instead of having it paid out through industry.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And you voted against it.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I did not vote against it at all. Apparently you did not know what you were voting for in the speech from the throne, and apparently you do not know even yet. For the edification of some of these individuals who do not understand what the speech from the throne is, 1 shall

refer again to the debate in reply to the speech from the throne, and the reference at page 259 of Hansard for February 8, 1944, to the subject of family allowances.
How people can be so stupid as to be able to read and not understand simple English is quite beyond my comprehension. If the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek had turned to page 259 of Hansard of 1944 he would have read this-and these are my own words:
That purchasing power can be made up in several ways. A large portion of it can be supplied through industry, which pays the wages and salaries, but there is never enough paid out by industry in wages and salaries to begin to buy back the products of industry, and so there is always a lag. We have advocated the issue of national dividends to make up that lag. Every other party in the house has criticized and ridiculed this principle of national dividends. In view of that, it is amazing now to see in the speech from the throne mention made of family allowances.
It will be noted that I used the proper expression when I said that mention was made of it, but no proposal was ever included in that address; and that is where the hon. member's mind has been wandering.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: His beard got caught in the previous page.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I quote further:
In view of that, it is amazing now to see in the speech from the throne mention made of family allowances. I have not heard anybody criticize them. Family allowances are in part a national dividend, but only to a very selected portion of our citizens. I am waiting with a great deal of interest to hear what the rank and file of the
The Budget-Mr. C. E. Johnston Liberals supporting the party which proposed these family allowances have to say about that.
This is the part of my speech to which I draw the attention of the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek:
The principle of the family allowance is sound.
We have never taken any other stand.
Then, Mr. Speaker, when we come to page 362 of Hansard for February 10, 1944, we find the vote recorded and, of course, as this was a non-confidence motion we voted nonconfidence in the government.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
You voted against
family allowances.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order. It being ten o'clock, perhaps this would be a convenient place for the hon. member to move the adjournment of the debate.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, because I am now turning my remarks from the address in 1944 to the problem to which it refers, namely the family allowances measure.
On motion of Mr. Johnston (Bow River) the debate was adjourned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we are enjoying this so much we shall go on tomorrow.
At ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Wednesday, May 11, 1955
